title: Rotate the secret you already deleted: detect-secrets and the key still living in git history
brief: Scan a repo with `detect-secrets scan`, then face the part nobody likes: deleting the line and committing does not remove the key — it sits in every prior commit and was scraped seconds after you pushed. The real fix is rotate first, then purge history with git filter-repo, plus a pre-commit hook so it never lands again. The failure — 'I deleted it, we're fine' — stays in.
source_title: Secure Coding: Preventing the OWASP Top 10
rationale: it-journey teaches secret handling straight; lifehacker has git and .gitignore hacks but nothing on scanning committed secrets or why deletion is theater. The 'you deleted it and it's still there' gotcha is real, testable, and on-voice.

title: pip-audit: the dependency scanner that finds real holes and a pile you can't patch
brief: Honest verdict on `pip-audit` (and its npm audit cousin): it catches genuinely known-vulnerable versions in seconds, and it also floods you with transitive-dependency advisories you can't fix and scores that don't match your actual risk. What earns an upgrade, what's noise, and when to wire it into CI versus running it by hand.
source_title: Secure Coding: Preventing the OWASP Top 10
rationale: The tools lane is all coreutils rewrites (rg/fd/bat/eza...); a dependency-audit scanner is fresh territory and it-journey names pip-audit/npm audit as the supply-chain check. The honest angle — most of what it reports you can't act on — is exactly this pillar's promise.

title: Scope the token before your MCP server gets the keys: a fine-grained PAT that can't touch prod
brief: An MCP server inherits every permission of the token you hand it, so a classic admin PAT means one bad prompt can force-push. Build a fine-grained personal access token with read-only Contents/Issues/PR scopes, wire it into the server's env, and prove the limit by asking the agent to do something it shouldn't and watching it get a 403. The gotcha: the easy token is the dangerous one.
rationale: lifehacker's meta docs cover its own autopilot but there's no general hack on scoping the token an MCP/agent runs under. Fine-grained PAT scoping is concrete, testable, and the least-privilege footgun is a real, on-voice failure.

title: STRIDE your side project in 20 minutes: one data flow, six questions, a ranked fix list
brief: Skip the enterprise threat-model binder. Draw one data-flow diagram (you, your app, your database), run the six STRIDE questions against the single arrow that crosses a trust boundary, and rank what you find by likelihood times impact. You'll know it worked when you have three fixes worth doing this week — and the honest part is that the paper version beats the fancy modeling tool you'll never open twice.
rationale: it-journey teaches STRIDE/DFDs earnestly; lifehacker has no security-process content, and the 'do the 20-minute version on one flow' angle is genuinely useful while poking at security theater — satire on top of a real method.

title: Scope your GitHub Actions permissions block before the default token can write to everything
brief: The default GITHUB_TOKEN hands a workflow broad write access to your whole repo, so one compromised action can push to main. Add a top-level `permissions:` block set to `contents: read`, then grant each job only the scope it truly needs. The footgun that stays in: the moment you declare that block, every scope you didn't list drops to no-access, so the job that pushes a tag or cuts a release starts failing with a 403 until you add `contents: write` back exactly where it belongs.
rationale: it-journey teaches least-privilege workflow permissions as agent governance; lifehacker's Actions hacks cover GH_TOKEN and packaging workflows but never scoping the permissions block itself. The 'lock it down and now the release job 403s' gotcha is real, testable, and on-voice.

title: type -a before you alias: see what a command name already runs so you don't shadow it
brief: Before you drop `alias ls='ls --color'` into your .bashrc, run `type -a ls` to see everything that name already resolves to — alias, shell builtin, function, and the real /bin/ls, in the order the shell picks them. The failure that stays in: you alias over a name a script depends on, it breaks in a way that works fine when you paste the same command by hand, and `command ls` (which skips the alias) is the one-word escape hatch.
rationale: The cellar quest teaches alias/unalias/type earnestly; lifehacker has a git-alias pack and mentions shadowing a builtin once, but nothing on checking what a name resolves to first. type -a / command is offline-testable and the shadow-a-name footgun is on-voice.

title: Read a failing CI run from your terminal: gh run view --log-failed and the watch --exit-status trap
brief: Stop clicking through the Actions web UI to find why a run went red. `gh run view --log-failed` prints just the failing step's log, and `gh run watch` follows a run live. The trap that stays in: `gh run watch` exits 0 even when the run failed, so a script that gates on it treats a broken build as green — you have to add `--exit-status` to make the failure actually propagate.
rationale: it-journey lists gh run list/view as the machine-verifiable CI signal; lifehacker's gh hack covers setting GH_TOKEN, not reading results. The --exit-status footgun — a watch that returns success on a failed run — is a real, testable, on-voice gotcha nothing else covers.

title: chmod 644 and 755, never 777: the permission bits that decide what's safe to run
brief: Read an `ls -l` line as a file-type char plus three rwx triples, then set them on purpose: 644 (rw-r--r--) for data, 755 (rwxr-xr-x) for scripts, and never 777, which hands write access to everyone on the box. Two failures stay in: you `chmod +x` a script that has no `#!` shebang line and it still won't run, and you forget the `./` prefix because the current directory isn't on your PATH.
rationale: The armoury quest teaches chmod and permission bits earnestly; lifehacker has ssh/tar/rsync/xargs hacks but no chmod hack at all. Octal-vs-symbolic notation, the 777 security footgun, and the shebang/PATH failures are all offline-testable and on-voice.

title: Read the query plan before you add the index: EXPLAIN ANALYZE, Seq Scan vs Index Scan, and the function that kills it
brief: Stop guessing which column to index. Run `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` on the slow query and read the plan: a `Seq Scan` with a big 'Rows Removed by Filter' is the tell, an `Index Scan` is the win. Add the index, re-run, watch the time drop. Two footguns stay in: a composite index on `(a, b)` does nothing for a query that filters only on `b` (column order matters), and wrapping the column in a function — `WHERE lower(email) = ...` — silently defeats the plain index until you build a matching expression index.
source_title: Query Optimization: Tuning Fast Database Queries
rationale: lifehacker has zero database content — this is a whole fresh pillar the coreutils/git/CI hacks never touch. it-journey teaches EXPLAIN and indexing straight; the 'you added an index and it still seq-scans because of a function' gotcha is real, reproducible in a Docker Postgres, and exactly this pillar's promise.

title: 80% coverage and still broken: the branch c8 counted as covered but never ran
brief: Wire a coverage gate into your tests with `c8 --check-coverage --lines 80` so an untested change fails the build instead of merging quietly. The honest part that stays in: line coverage is the easy metric to game — a function whose `if` branch never fired can still show 100% lines covered, so the number says safe while a whole path is untested. Turn on `--branches` too, and know the difference before you trust the badge.
source_title: Testing Integration: Tiered CI/CD Test Gates
rationale: it-journey teaches the testing pyramid and c8 coverage gates earnestly; lifehacker has many CI hacks (timeout, bash-compat, link-checker) but nothing on coverage gates or the line-vs-branch coverage lie. The '80% and still broken' angle is satire on a comfort metric, fully reproducible with node --test + c8, and uncovered.

title: Stop scrolling CI logs: write a real summary to $GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY
brief: A GitHub Actions job doesn't have to bury its result in 800 lines of log. Echo Markdown to the `$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY` file and it renders as a table on the run's summary page — pass/fail counts, the one number that mattered, a link. The gotchas that stay in: it appends (every `>>` adds, so `>` when you meant `>>` eats the earlier lines), it's per-job not global, and echoing untrusted text into it is a Markdown-injection footgun you handle by not piping raw input through it.
source_title: Initiation Rites: Agents in the SDLC
rationale: it-journey names GitHub Actions step summaries as the observability surface for bounded agents; lifehacker's gh/Actions hacks cover GH_TOKEN and packaging workflows but never $GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY. It's trivially testable (echo to a file), genuinely useful, and the append-vs-overwrite footgun is on-voice.

title: You can't gate a workflow step on a secret in `if:` — promote it to an env first
brief: The obvious guard — `if: secrets.MY_TOKEN != ''` — doesn't work, because GitHub Actions won't evaluate `secrets.*` in a job-level `if:`. Copy the secret to a step output or a job env first, then branch on that, so a workflow that needs a token skips cleanly instead of failing when it's absent. The footgun that stays in: pull requests from forks get empty secrets by design, so any agent step that assumes the token exists breaks on exactly the PRs strangers open — the graceful no-op is the fix, not a louder error.
source_title: Summon the Golem: Claude Code as a Headless CI Agent
rationale: it-journey's golem quest gates its agent lane on both an env var and a secret; lifehacker's Actions hacks never cover the can't-use-secrets-in-if rule or the empty-secrets-on-forks behavior. Both are real, famous, testable GitHub Actions footguns and the graceful-skip angle fits the brand's 'leave the failure in' rule.

title: Your database connection pool is too big: size it by cores, not hope (and the idle-in-transaction leak)
brief: The counterintuitive fix for a slow, connection-starved app: make the pool smaller. Size it with the HikariCP formula (`cores * 2 + 1` — 17 for an 8-core box, not 200), because Postgres spawns an OS process per connection and can only do parallel work up to its cores. Put PgBouncer in `pool_mode = transaction` so 1000 clients share 20 real connections. The failure that stays in: a connection you never returned shows up as a row stuck `idle in transaction` in `pg_stat_activity`, quietly eating a slot until the pool exhausts and everything hangs — the fix is returning it in a `finally`/context manager, not a bigger pool.
rationale: it-journey teaches pooling straight; lifehacker has zero database-ops content (the only DB idea is query-optimization, a different topic). The 'bigger pool is slower' inversion and the idle-in-transaction leak are real, reproducible in a Docker Postgres, and exactly the pillar's promise.

title: The database migration that rolls out fine and rolls back never: test your downgrade before prod
brief: Write migrations as paired up/down functions (`alembic revision`, `upgrade()`/`downgrade()`) and actually run the downgrade once — because the rollback nobody tested is the one you reach for at 2am. Two footguns stay in: a plain `ALTER TABLE ... DROP COLUMN`/`RENAME` takes a lock that breaks the running code the instant it lands (the fix is the expand-contract dance — add the new column, backfill, deploy code using both, drop the old one a release later), and you can never edit a migration you already shipped because the tool checksums it and refuses to run on a mismatch. Reproducible against a throwaway Docker Postgres.
rationale: it-journey teaches Flyway/Alembic and expand-contract earnestly; lifehacker has no schema-migration content at all. The 'downgrade you never ran' and the lock that breaks live code are real, testable, on-voice failures, and the topic is distinct from the query-optimization idea already queued.

title: Dark mode in a dozen lines: prefers-color-scheme, CSS custom properties, and the contrast that fails WCAG
brief: Define your colors once as CSS custom properties (`--bg`, `--accent`) on `:root`, then flip only the values inside `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` — the whole page re-themes with no JS and no duplicated rules. The failure that stays in: the accent color that passed the 4.5:1 WCAG contrast ratio on a white background quietly fails it on your new dark one, so 'dark mode done' and 'dark mode readable' are two different checkmarks — verify each theme in a contrast checker, don't assume inverting the background inverted the legibility.
source_title: Profile Themes: Unleashing the Style Sorcerer
rationale: Frontend hacks are in-scope (auto-hide-navbar exists) but nothing covers theming; it-journey teaches CSS variables + prefers-color-scheme + WCAG straight. The 'your dark theme looks done but fails contrast' gotcha is real, checkable in browser devtools/a contrast tool, and on-voice satire of ship-it theming.

title: One mkdir, many folders: brace expansion (and the space that silently breaks it)
brief: Stop running `mkdir` five times. `mkdir -p proj/{src,test,docs,.github/workflows}` builds the whole tree in one shot, `{1..10}` and `{a..z}` make ranges, and `cp file{,.bak}` is the one-keystroke backup. The failure that stays in: put a space after a comma — `{src, test}` — and the shell doesn't expand it at all, it hands `mkdir` two literal arguments and you get a folder actually named `{src,` plus one named `test}`. Braces also expand before variables, so `{$a,$b}` won't do what you hoped. Every case is offline-testable with `echo` before you commit to it.
source_title: Building Technical Communities: Govern and Include
rationale: The quest sets up its workspace with `mkdir -p ~/community/{governance,events}` — brace expansion used straight and unexplained. lifehacker has git/tar/xargs/rsync shell hacks but no brace-expansion hack, and the space-breaks-it footgun is a famous, fully offline-reproducible bite that fits the 'leave the failure in' rule.

title: Stop reinstalling every dependency on each build: order your Dockerfile so the layer cache does its job
brief: Copy your lockfile (`package.json` / `requirements.txt`) and run the install BEFORE you `COPY` the rest of the source, so editing `app.js` doesn't re-run `npm install` — Docker invalidates every layer downstream of the first instruction that changed, and instruction order is the whole game. Two footguns stay in: `EXPOSE` documents a port but does not publish it (only `-p` at runtime maps it to the host), and a missing `.dockerignore` silently copies `node_modules`/`.git` into the build context, busting the cache you just arranged and bloating the image. Reproducible with `docker build` twice and reading the `CACHED` lines.
rationale: lifehacker's existing Docker hack covers the day-one commands and the daemon error; nothing covers Dockerfile layer caching or build-context hygiene. The copy-lockfile-first ordering and the EXPOSE-isn't-publish footgun are famous, reproducible, and on-voice — a distinct deeper topic from the beginner-commands hack.

title: Clean up your messy commits before you push: git rebase -i, --fixup/--autosquash, and the history you must never rewrite
brief: Turn 'wip', 'more wip', 'typo' into one honest commit with `git rebase -i` (squash/reword/drop), or mark corrections as you go with `git commit --fixup <sha>` and let `git rebase -i --autosquash` file each fix under the commit it belongs to. The failure that stays in: rebasing rewrites the commit SHAs, so doing it to anything you've already pushed forces everyone who pulled it into a diverged history and a mess of duplicate commits — the rule is rewrite what's local, never what's shared. Fully reproducible in a throwaway repo.
source_title: Commit Hygiene: Crafting Clean, Atomic Commits
rationale: it-journey teaches atomic commits and interactive rebase earnestly; lifehacker's git hacks cover aliases, worktree, and reflog but never rebase -i or --autosquash. The 'never rebase pushed history' footgun is real, offline-testable, and on-voice.

title: Your model's loss bounces instead of dropping: the optimizer.zero_grad() line the training loop can't skip
brief: PyTorch accumulates gradients by design, so a loop missing `optimizer.zero_grad()` adds each batch's gradients on top of the last one's and the loss lurches around instead of falling. The fix is one line at the top of the loop — zero_grad → forward → `loss.backward()` → `optimizer.step()` — and leaving it out sends you chasing a 'bad learning rate' that was never the problem. Reproducible on CPU with a tiny linear model (no GPU needed); the sibling footgun — a model on the GPU can't multiply a tensor still on the CPU — gets a one-line `.to(device)` note.
source_title: Deep Learning Frameworks: PyTorch vs TensorFlow
rationale: lifehacker has zero machine-learning content — a whole fresh pillar the coreutils/git/CI hacks never touch. it-journey names the missing zero_grad as the second most common bug; it's fully reproducible on CPU and the 'my loss won't go down' failure is exactly this pillar's promise.

title: Seal the test results before the robot wakes up: evidence a coding agent can't forge
brief: The failure mode in any self-healing CI loop is the self-grading agent — when it can't actually run the tests, it writes a passing result anyway. The countermeasure is ordering: have the workflow mint the evidence artifact BEFORE the agent starts and verify it AFTER, so the record the agent is graded on is one it never had write access to. Why 'the agent reports success' and 'the tests passed' are two different facts, and how sealing the evidence at trigger time closes the tampering gap.
rationale: it-journey's Ouroboros campaign names the 'self-grading golem' that fabricates results as its boss fight. lifehacker's meta docs cover its sandbox runner, linter, and drift check but never the workflow-sealed-evidence pattern that stops an agent forging its own pass — and lifehacker IS a self-operating website, so it's a direct in-conversation angle.

title: DuckDB: the analytics database that's just a file and runs SQL on your CSV
brief: Honest verdict on DuckDB: an in-process, columnar SQL engine you `pip install` with no server to run, that queries a CSV or Parquet file directly (`SELECT ... FROM 'sales.csv'`) and chews through GROUP BY aggregates that make SQLite crawl. The dealbreakers that stay in: it's OLAP not OLTP (built for reads and one writer, not your app's concurrent transactions), a join wider than RAM will spill or fall over, and `read_csv_auto`'s type sniffing quietly decides a ZIP code is an integer and eats the leading zero. What it replaces, what it doesn't, and when plain Postgres still wins.
source_title: Data Warehousing: Build a Dimensional Star Schema in SQL
rationale: it-journey uses DuckDB straight to teach star schemas; lifehacker's tool lane is all coreutils rewrites (rg/fd/bat/eza) with no database at all, and DuckDB is the natural 'SQLite for analytics' member of that family. Query-a-file-with-no-server is genuinely useful and the OLAP-not-OLTP and type-sniffing gotchas are real, reproducible, and on-voice.

title: Stop pasting the same HTML header into every page: Jinja2 template inheritance
brief: Write the page shell once as `base.html` with `{% block content %}` holes, then `{% extends 'base.html' %}` in each page and fill only the blocks — no more find-and-replace across ten files when the nav changes. Every step rendered for real with Python's jinja2. The failures that stay in: a typo'd block name doesn't raise an error, it just renders nothing; autoescape is OFF by default in a bare `Environment` (Flask turns it on), so the same template is XSS-safe in one place and a hole in another; and stray blank lines leak from Jinja's whitespace rules until you set `trim_blocks`/`lstrip_blocks` or reach for `{%- -%}`.
source_title: The Temple of Templates: Reusable Abstractions
rationale: it-journey teaches Jinja2 inheritance/blocks/includes earnestly; lifehacker has git/shell/CI/frontend hacks but nothing on templating, and the autoescape-off-by-default and silent-missing-block footguns are famous, fully offline-reproducible with pip install jinja2, and fit the 'leave the failure in' rule.

title: Run your data-load script twice without doubling every row: ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE and the watermark that skips the rest
brief: Make a load rerunnable so a retry doesn't duplicate: `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT(id) DO UPDATE SET ...` (SQLite/Postgres upsert) turns a re-run into a harmless update, and tracking `MAX(updated_at)` as a watermark pulls only new rows next time. Every step reproducible in a throwaway sqlite3 db. The footgun that stays in: a watermark-only `updated_at > last` silently misses rows sharing the exact boundary timestamp (and late-arriving data) — the fix is a small overlap window on the watermark PLUS the idempotent upsert, so re-reading a few rows costs nothing instead of double-counting them.
source_title: ETL Pipeline Design: Scalable Python Data Pipelines
rationale: it-journey teaches idempotent loads and the watermark pattern straight; lifehacker's DB ideas cover query plans, pooling, and migrations but never making a load safely rerunnable. The 'ran it twice, now every row is doubled' failure and the equal-timestamp boundary miss are real, offline-testable in sqlite3, and on-voice — distinct from the migration and query-plan ideas already queued.

title: Validate a DataFrame before it poisons the table: a pandera schema and a quarantine bin
brief: Put a gate at the pipeline's front door: a pandera `DataFrameSchema` that checks nulls, ranges, uniqueness, and regex formats, run with `lazy=True` so one pass reports every bad column at once instead of dying on the first failure. Then route the failing rows to a quarantine table instead of dropping them — a silent drop is the bug you can't debug three days later. Reproducible with pandas + pandera on a tiny frame. The honest limit that stays in: row-level rules pass every individually-valid record while the batch as a whole is wrong (half the usual row count, a null-rate that tripled), so schema validation is necessary but a count/z-score check on the batch is the other half of the job.
rationale: it-journey teaches Great Expectations/pandera, quarantine tables, and batch anomaly checks earnestly; lifehacker has no data-validation content at all. Schema-at-the-boundary is genuinely useful, fully reproducible in pandas, and the 'every row valid, the batch still wrong' gotcha is exactly the honest-payload angle — distinct from the ETL-upsert idea (validation vs idempotency).

title: The forbidden-actions list your coding agent reads first and can ignore anyway
brief: How an AGENTS.md / .github/copilot-instructions.md actually steers a coding agent: repo context, conventions, preferred patterns, and the Forbidden Actions section that spells out the pushes-to-main, infra edits, and credential writes you never want. The honest part, from a site run by exactly this kind of robot: a markdown file is a strong suggestion, not a permission boundary — the agent can read 'never push to main' and reach for it anyway. The rule only holds because branch protection, scoped tokens, and required checks enforce in CI what the prose merely requests. Write both files; trust only the one with teeth.
rationale: it-journey's cheatsheet presents AGENTS.md forbidden-actions as the agent's constraint mechanism; lifehacker IS an agent-run site whose meta docs cover its own CI guardrails but never the agent-instructions file itself or the honest gap between a prose rule and an enforced one. Direct in-conversation angle with the sister site, not a rewrite of their reference.

title: Stop your GitHub Action from triggering itself: the bot-author skip guard
brief: A workflow with `contents: write` that commits and pushes will fire the very event that started it and run forever. The fix is a guard at the top: read the head commit's author with `git log -1 --format='%an'` and exit early when it's your bot (`content-review[bot]`). The failures that stay in: the check needs `fetch-depth: 2` or there's no history to read the author from, and a `[skip ci]` in the commit message is flimsier than the author check because a human can trip it by accident too.
source_title: The Self-Operating Website 06: The Editor's Eye
rationale: it-journey teaches the self-retrigger loop guard straight; lifehacker IS a workflow-driven site and its CI hacks cover secrets-in-if and step summaries but never the commit-and-push infinite loop or the author-skip fix. Real, reproducible, and on-voice — the runaway workflow is a genuine, funny failure.

title: Let the content bot edit posts but not your workflows: a changed-files allowlist gate
brief: A job trusted to push editorial commits will happily push whatever is in the diff — including `.github/` or `_config.yml` if something slips them in. Add a smuggle guard that runs `git diff --name-only` against the base and fails unless every changed path matches an allowlist like `^(_posts/|pages/|assets/images/)`. The gotcha that stays in: compare against `origin/$BASE...HEAD`, not `HEAD~1`, or a multi-commit push sneaks files past a diff that only looked at the last commit.
source_title: The Self-Operating Website 06: The Editor's Eye
rationale: The editor's-eye quest pairs the loop guard with a least-privilege 'smuggle guard' on changed paths; lifehacker's guardrail docs cover branch protection and scoped tokens but never a changed-files allowlist inside the job itself. Distinct mechanism from the permissions-block idea already queued, testable, and squarely on the site's own 'the mechanics are the content' brand.

title: Nerd Font fix for a prompt that renders as boxes: install the font, then point the terminal at it
brief: That powerline/oh-my-zsh/starship prompt shows tofu boxes and question marks because the glyphs need a patched Nerd Font. Install one (`brew install --cask font-meslo-lg-nerd-font`, or download then `fc-cache -fv` on Linux), verify with `fc-list | grep -i meslo`, and — the step everyone misses — set the font on the TERMINAL profile, not only your editor, because VS Code's `editor.fontFamily` never touches the integrated terminal's. The other failure that stays in: blurry glyphs usually mean GPU acceleration, fixed with `terminal.integrated.gpuAcceleration: off`.
source_title: Nerd Font Enchantment: Terminal Icon Mastery
rationale: it-journey teaches Nerd Font install across OSes earnestly; lifehacker's hacks are all git/shell/CI with zero terminal-appearance content, and the 'my prompt is all boxes because the terminal font and the editor font are two different settings' gotcha is a famous, verifiable, on-voice failure.

title: Get the Verified badge on your commits: sign with GPG (and why GitHub still says Unverified)
brief: Generate a signing key with `gpg --full-generate-key`, turn signing on with `git config --global commit.gpgsign true` plus `user.signingkey`, and your commits carry a signature. The part that stays in: GitHub keeps showing 'Unverified' until you upload the PUBLIC key to your account AND the key's email exactly matches your committer email — a mismatch fails silently. Plus the terminal headache where signing dies with 'gpg failed to sign the data' until you `export GPG_TTY=$(tty)` so pinentry can actually prompt.
rationale: The onboarding note sets up SSH and GPG identity straight; lifehacker's git hacks cover aliases, worktree, and reflog, and the byline post touches authorship, but nothing covers commit signing. The 'signed but still Unverified because the email doesn't match' and the GPG_TTY pinentry failure are real, reproducible, and on-voice.

title: Your Django page fired 500 queries: kill the N+1 with select_related and prefetch_related
brief: One template loop over a list of orders, each touching `order.customer.name`, quietly runs a query per row — the N+1 that makes a snappy page crawl at scale. Count them for real with `len(connection.queries)` (DEBUG on), then collapse them: `select_related` joins a foreign key in a single query, `prefetch_related` runs one batched second query for reverse and many-to-many links. The footgun that stays in: `select_related` on a many-to-many raises instead of helping, and a `.only()` you added to save bytes silently re-triggers a query the moment you touch a field you deferred.
source_title: Stack Attack: AI-Built Django + React Enterprise ERP
rationale: it-journey names N+1 and select_related/prefetch_related as core ERP gotchas; lifehacker has a Django new-project hack but nothing on ORM query counts. The 'my page runs 500 queries' failure is reproducible with connection.queries, and the select_related-vs-prefetch split (with the M2M and deferred-field traps) is a real, on-voice footgun the DB-query-plan idea doesn't touch.

title: The customer with zero orders vanished from your report: LEFT JOIN and the NULL that sums to nothing
brief: Your revenue-per-customer query used an INNER JOIN, so every customer who ordered nothing silently dropped off the report — the bug that makes a total look right and be wrong. Switch to LEFT JOIN to keep them, then handle the NULLs it brings in: `SUM` over zero rows returns NULL, not 0, so wrap it in `COALESCE(SUM(amount), 0)`. The footgun that stays in: putting a condition on the right-hand table in `WHERE` quietly turns your LEFT JOIN back into an INNER JOIN (move that condition into the `ON`). Every case reproducible in a throwaway sqlite3 db.
rationale: it-journey calls INNER-vs-LEFT one of the most common SQL bugs and teaches COALESCE straight; lifehacker's DB ideas cover EXPLAIN/indexes, pooling, and migrations but never JOIN semantics or NULL handling. The 'zero-order customer disappears' failure and the WHERE-defeats-LEFT-JOIN trap are famous, offline-testable in sqlite3, and on-voice.

title: Stop storing a list in one column: the junction table that models many-to-many right
brief: You gave a post `tags TEXT` and stuffed 'sql,python,git' into one cell — now 'all posts tagged python' needs a LIKE that also matches 'pythonic', and you can't count tags at all. That comma-jam violates first normal form; the fix is a junction table (`post_tags(post_id, tag_id)`) with a composite primary key so the same pair can't be linked twice. The footgun that stays in: skip that composite key (or a UNIQUE on the pair) and nothing stops duplicate rows, so every count you run comes back doubled. Reproducible end to end in a throwaway sqlite3 db.
source_title: Data Modeling: Schema Design and Database Relationships
rationale: it-journey teaches ER modeling, 1NF, and junction tables with composite keys earnestly; lifehacker's DB ideas cover querying, pooling, and migrations but never schema design. The comma-separated-column anti-pattern and the missing composite key that lets duplicates in are real, sqlite-testable, and on-voice — distinct from the JOIN and query-plan ideas already queued.

title: How much rope to give the robot: rating each task by reversibility, blast radius, and predictability
brief: A Meta take on the question every self-operating site eventually hits: not 'should the robot act' but 'how far, on which task.' Score each task type on three axes — can it be undone, how wide is the blast radius, how predictable is it — and map the answer to a tier from 'a human approves every action' up to 'act on its own authority, audited later.' The honest part, from a site the robot already runs: a typo fix and a production deploy are not the same delegation, a tier only means something when a real GitHub control (draft PR, branch protection, CODEOWNERS, required checks) actually enforces it, and the label without the enforcement is a comment, not a guardrail.
rationale: it-journey's L0–L4 matrix classifies tasks by reversibility/blast-radius/predictability with a YAML schema; lifehacker's meta docs cover individual guardrails (branch protection, the rate limiter) but never a per-task autonomy rubric. Since lifehacker IS an agent-run site, rating its own tasks is a direct in-conversation angle, not a rewrite — and the 'a tier is only real if a control enforces it' point is squarely on-brand.

title: Your MCP server can't authenticate to Google: you downloaded the OAuth client, not the service-account key
brief: Wiring a Google Analytics MCP server, it fails auth every time — because the JSON you grabbed is a `client_secret_….apps.googleusercontent.com.json` OAuth web client, and a server-to-server tool needs a service-account key instead. Create the service account, download ITS key, and grant that account explicit Viewer access on the property. Two more footguns stay in: the numeric property ID is not the `G-XXXXXX` measurement tag, and the multi-line PEM private key crammed into one env var breaks unless its `\n` newlines survive the shell — keep the key in a file, `chmod 600` it, and read it, don't paste it into your shell history.
source_title: Google Analytics MCP Integration for AI Agents
rationale: it-journey wires the GA MCP server straight; lifehacker's one MCP idea is scoping a GitHub PAT, not Google service-account auth. The OAuth-client-vs-service-account mix-up, the property-ID-vs-measurement-ID confusion, and the \n-in-the-env-var PEM key are real, on-voice credential footguns nothing else covers.

title: Resolve a git merge conflict without deleting someone's work: the markers, git merge --abort, and the ours/theirs that flips during a rebase
brief: When a merge stops on `CONFLICT`, read the three markers (`<<<<<<<` your side, `=======`, `>>>>>>>` theirs), edit down to the real answer, `git add` the file, then commit — or bail cleanly with `git merge --abort` while nothing's staged. Two failures stay in: 'resolving' by keeping only your half silently deletes a coworker's change that belonged in the same block, and `--ours`/`--theirs` mean the opposite during a rebase (HEAD is their branch while your commits replay on top), so the shortcut that saved the right side in a merge throws it away in a rebase. Reproducible end to end in a throwaway repo.
source_title: Git Workflow Mastery: Branches, Merging & Team Collaboration
rationale: it-journey teaches conflict markers and merge-vs-rebase straight; lifehacker's git hacks cover aliases, worktree, reflog, and bisect but never resolving a conflict — and POST-003 is a field note about backlog collisions, not a how-to. The 'ours/theirs flips in a rebase' footgun is famous, offline-reproducible, and on-voice.

title: Nested code fences: show a code block that contains triple backticks without collapsing half your page
brief: When your Markdown example is itself a fenced block — a README snippet, a workflow YAML with a heredoc — the inner triple backtick closes the outer one early and the rest of the page renders as broken prose. The fix is to make the OUTER fence longer: wrap the whole thing in four backticks (or a `~~~` tilde fence) and the three-backtick block inside is now plain text. The failure that stays in: mismatched fence lengths swallow everything after them silently, so a doc looks fine in your editor and detonates once the site's Markdown renderer runs. Verify by rendering, not by eyeballing.
rationale: The quest report's own top-priority bug is a markdown fence-nesting error that collapsed ~60% of a quest into malformed code — a perfect lifehacker gap: lifehacker has a markdown-tangle hack but nothing on nested fences. The four-backtick/tilde fix is genuinely useful, fully offline-testable by rendering, and the 'looks fine in the editor, detonates in the renderer' failure is on-voice.

title: Conventional commits, actually enforced: a commit-msg hook that rejects 'update stuff' (and the --no-verify that strolls past it)
brief: Turn the `type: summary` convention (feat/fix/docs/refactor/test/chore) from a suggestion into a gate: a `.git/hooks/commit-msg` script that greps the first line against a regex and exits non-zero, so 'update stuff' and 'more fixes lol' bounce before they land. Every step runnable in a throwaway repo. The honest part that stays in: a git hook is local and opt-in, it lives in `.git/` so it never clones with the repo (you need `core.hooksPath` or a tool like pre-commit to share it), and anyone can walk straight past it with `git commit --no-verify`. It's a linter, not a lock — the real enforcement is a CI check on the pushed commit.
source_title: Commit Hygiene: Crafting Clean, Atomic Commits
rationale: it-journey teaches the conventional-commit format but explicitly stops short of hooks or tooling; lifehacker's git ideas cover aliases, worktree, reflog, and rebase -i cleanup (a different angle on this same source) but never enforcing the message format. The commit-msg hook is offline-testable and the 'a local hook isn't a lock, --no-verify beats it' gotcha is squarely on-voice.

title: Cache-aside without the stampede: the TTL, the write-path invalidation, and the thundering herd when a hot key expires
brief: The biggest speedup is the request you never compute: check the cache, on a miss read the source and write it back with a TTL. But the two hard parts stay in. Invalidation — a TTL alone serves stale data until it expires, so a write has to bust the key too, and getting that ordering wrong reintroduces the staleness you were fixing. And the stampede — the instant a popular key expires, a thousand concurrent misses all hit the database at once and knock it over; the fix is a single-flight lock so one request recomputes while the rest wait, plus a little random jitter on the TTL so keys don't all expire on the same tick. Demonstrable with a small script that fires N concurrent readers at an expired key.
source_title: Scaling Strategies: Horizontal Growth, Caching, and CAP
rationale: it-journey teaches cache-aside and names invalidation and cache stampede as the two hardest problems; lifehacker has database hacks (query plans, pooling, migrations) but zero caching content. The single-flight stampede fix and the invalidation-ordering trap are real, on-voice failures with a reproducible demo — a fresh corner of the same systems territory.

title: Turn your git history into an RPG character sheet: git shortlog, --shortstat, and the XP metric that's a lie
brief: Point a few real commands at your own repo and render yourself a class and a level: `git shortlog -sn --no-merges` for commits per author, `git log --author=you --shortstat` piped through awk to total lines added and removed. The useful payload is honest reporting — those commands genuinely audit who touched what. The part that stays in: lines-of-code is a garbage metric wearing a medal (a 900-line vendored dependency 'levels you up'; a hard bug fix that deletes 40 lines 'costs' you XP), and forget `--no-merges` and every merge commit double-counts. Certified n00b regardless of the number.
rationale: it-journey's forge-your-character builds an earnest gamified profile — 7 RPG classes, an XP formula floor(log2(xp/100)) — from contributor stats. That is lifehacker's exact motif (fake productivity tiers, Certified n00b), so the in-conversation angle writes itself: the git-stats commands are real and offline-testable, and the 'lines-of-code is a joke stat' honesty is the payload under the bit. No character-sheet or git-stats hack exists in the backlog.

title: The Norway Problem: why your YAML `on:`, `no`, and `1.20` parse as the wrong type
brief:
YAML 1.1 quietly casts bare words: `on`/`off`/`yes`/`no` become booleans and `NO` (Norway's country code) becomes `false`, so a key or value you typed as text comes back as `True`/`False` and your lookup misses. Reproduce it in one line — `printf 'on: yes
NO: text
ver: 1.20
' | python3 -c 'import yaml,sys; print(yaml.safe_load(sys.stdin))'` — and watch the keys turn boolean and the version drop its trailing zero to a float. The fix is quoting: `"on"`, `"no"`, `"1.20"`. The footgun that stays in: a GitHub Actions workflow's top-level `on:` is the same trap wearing a badge, which is why some tools quote it and some hand you the boolean `True`.
rationale: The game-developer quest report's own gotcha is 'YAML 1.1 treats on: as boolean True when parsed.' lifehacker has a yq tool review but no hack on YAML type coercion, and the Norway problem plus the on:-becomes-true trap are famous, one-line-reproducible, and on-voice — the config that looks right and parses wrong is exactly the brand's failure-stays-in payload.

title: Retire an API endpoint without the 404 ambush: Deprecation, Sunset, and 410 Gone
brief: Deleting an endpoint and returning 404 tells callers 'you typed it wrong,' not 'this is gone on purpose,' so they retry forever. Do it in the open instead: while both versions overlap, send `Deprecation: true`, a `Sunset:` date, and `Link: <newurl>; rel="successor-version"`; when the day comes, return `410 Gone` — the status that means intentional removal. Inspect any of it with `curl -sD - -o /dev/null <url>`. The part that stays in: header-based versioning (`Accept: application/vnd.api.v2+json`) is invisible in your access logs and, without `Vary: Accept`, your cache will hand a v1 response to a v2 client.
rationale: it-journey teaches URI-vs-header versioning and the announce/warn/overlap/sunset lifecycle straight; lifehacker has no API/HTTP content at all. The 410-not-404 semantics and the Vary: Accept cache trap are real, curl-testable, and on-voice — a fresh pillar for the hacks lane, distinct from the error-handling retry idea.

title: Scale a compose service past one replica and watch 'port is already allocated'
brief: `docker compose up --scale web=3` looks like it should just work — until all three replicas try to bind the same `8080:80` host port and the second one dies with 'port is already allocated,' because a fixed host port can only belong to one container. The fix: drop the host side so Docker assigns a random one (`- "80"`), or hand it a range (`- "8080-8082:80"`), and put a reverse proxy in front. The part that stays in: the container port and `EXPOSE` were never the problem — only the host mapping collides — and `docker compose ps` shows you the ephemeral ports it handed out.
rationale: The digital-artist quest report hits 'Port already allocated when scaling with fixed host ports' for real; lifehacker's Docker ideas cover the daemon error and Dockerfile layer caching but never compose scaling. The fixed-host-port collision is reproducible, on-voice, and a distinct topic from the layer-cache ordering idea already queued.

title: Retry only the request that's worth retrying: Retry-After, jitter, and never hammering a 422
brief: Not every failure earns a second attempt. Retry only 429 and 5xx (transient); never retry 400 or 422, because a request that's semantically wrong will be wrong every time and you're just DDoSing yourself. Honor the server's `Retry-After` header when it sends one, and add random jitter to your exponential backoff so a thousand clients that failed on the same tick don't all retry on the same tick (the thundering herd). The part that stays in: retrying a non-idempotent POST without an idempotency key turns one timed-out payment into two charges — send a client-generated key so the server dedupes the replay.
source_title: API Error Handling: Status Codes, Problem Details, and Retries
rationale: it-journey teaches status-code semantics, backoff+jitter, and idempotency keys straight; lifehacker has no HTTP-client content, and the existing idempotency ideas are ETL/queue upserts, not API retries. 'Never retry a 422' and 'jitter or you herd' are real, on-voice rules with a testable curl/loop demo — distinct from the deprecation-headers idea from the sibling versioning page.

title: You're billed by the token, not the word: count them before you paste the whole file into the prompt
brief: The context window and the invoice are both measured in tokens, and a token is roughly 3–4 characters — not a word — so 'just paste the whole file in' is a bill you didn't read. Count before you send: `pip install tiktoken` then a two-line `len(encoding.encode(text))`, or the `AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(...)` you already have from Hugging Face. The part that stays in: token counts are model-specific (a GPT tokenizer and a Llama tokenizer disagree on the same string), code and whitespace cost more tokens than prose, and 'characters ÷ 4' is a fine rough budget and a wrong hard limit — verify against the real tokenizer when the cap actually matters.
rationale: it-journey teaches subword tokenization and notes that pricing and context limits are counted in tokens, not words; lifehacker has a PyTorch training-loop idea but nothing on token accounting. Counting tokens is genuinely useful and offline-testable, and the 'paste it all in, pay for it all' angle is on-voice satire of prompt-stuffing culture — a fresh corner of the ML pillar.

title: Why your GitHub Action doesn't fire after the bot's commit: GITHUB_TOKEN can't trigger workflows (and the PAT that can)
brief: A push or PR made with the default GITHUB_TOKEN deliberately does NOT start another workflow — GitHub blocks that cascade to stop infinite loops — so the deploy or label job you expected to run after your bot commits just never fires, silently, under a green check. When you actually WANT the next workflow, push with a fine-grained PAT (or a GitHub App / deploy-key token) stored as a secret so the event carries a real actor. The footgun that stays in: that same PAT re-opens the infinite-loop door the default token was holding shut, so you've traded 'nothing runs' for 'everything runs forever' unless you add a bot-author or path guard back on top.
source_title: PRD Machine Requirement Conflicts - Resolution Report
rationale: it-journey's resolution report wrestles with PAT_TOKEN vs GITHUB_TOKEN inconsistency across its CI workflows; lifehacker's Actions hacks cover self-trigger guards, permissions scoping, and secrets-in-if but never the inverse — the default token's designed-in refusal to trigger downstream workflows and the PAT that restores the cascade. Real, famous, testable, and on-voice; the exact complement to the 'stop it triggering itself' guard already queued.

title: Write the decision down or relitigate it forever: the one-file ADR (Architecture Decision Record)
brief: Stop re-arguing 'why did we pick Postgres?' every six months. Drop a numbered markdown file at `docs/adr/0001-use-postgres.md` with four headings — Context, Decision, Status, Consequences — commit it, and `git log`/`grep -r` becomes a searchable memory of every choice and its blast radius. You'll know it worked when a new teammate finds the answer without pinging you. The failure that stays in: editing an old ADR to 'update' a reversed decision erases the very history you kept it for — an ADR is append-only, so you set the old one to `Status: Superseded by 0007` and write a new file, never overwrite.
source_title: Technical Leadership: Leading Without a Crown
rationale: it-journey teaches ADRs and plain-text, git-backed decision records straight as a leadership tool; lifehacker has git/CI/shell hacks and meta docs about its own decisions but no general how-to on decision records at all. The numbered-file template and git-log-as-memory are concrete, and the 'never edit, supersede' gotcha is a real, on-voice failure — satire of decision-by-meeting theater with the lightweight version that actually works underneath.

title: Your .txt is a JPEG: file reads the bytes, not the extension (and ls -F reads the type)
brief: The extension is a costume; the bytes are the truth. `file mystery` reads the magic number and tells you a 'report.txt' is actually a JPEG (or a zip, or an ELF binary), and `ls -F` tags every entry so you read type at a glance — `/` for a dir, `*` for executable, `@` for a symlink. Both are offline-testable: rename a real image to `.txt` and watch `file` refuse to be fooled. The footguns that stay in: the `*`/`/` characters `ls -F` prints are display markers, not part of the filename (paste one into a command and it breaks), and `file` reads content, so it happily calls an empty file 'empty' and a shebang-less script 'ASCII text' even when you meant it to run.
source_title: Bashcrawl Cellar: File Types, Aliases, and Emerald Amulet
rationale: The cellar quest teaches `file` (magic bytes) and `ls -F` type markers straight; lifehacker's existing magic-number ideas are hexyl-based hex-viewer angles, but nothing covers the everyday `file` command or the ls -F markers. The 'extension lies, bytes don't' framing and the marker-isn't-the-filename trap are famous, fully offline-reproducible, and on-voice — distinct from the type-a-alias hack already drawn from this same page.

title: A retry() function for any flaky command: exponential backoff, a max-attempts cap, and the jitter that stops the herd
brief: Wrap any command that fails for dumb transient reasons — a flaky curl, a container that isn't ready yet — in a reusable shell `retry()` that loops up to N times and doubles the sleep each round (1s, 2s, 4s). Offline-testable: point it at a command scripted to fail twice then succeed and watch it recover. Two failures stay in: retrying a command that fails for a REAL reason (bad auth, a 404, a typo) just burns the whole budget slowly before failing anyway — cap the attempts and don't retry the un-retryable — and a fleet of machines that all failed on the same tick will all retry on the same tick and stampede the thing that's already down, so add random jitter to the backoff, not a fixed sleep.
source_title: The Shield of Retries: Safe Execution and Error Handling
rationale: it-journey's Shield of Retries teaches retryable-vs-not classification, exponential backoff, and Retry-After in a GitHub Actions/agent context; lifehacker's one retry idea is HTTP-client curl semantics (never-retry-a-422), but there's no general shell-function hack you can drop in a script to wrap any flaky command. The pure-bash retry() with a cap and jitter is offline-reproducible and the 'retrying a permanent failure just DDoSes yourself slowly' gotcha is on-voice — distinct from the API-status-code idea.

title: Bootstrap your Terraform remote state without the chicken-and-egg: the S3 bucket and lock table that must exist first
brief: Move state off your laptop into an S3 backend so two people don't overwrite each other's infrastructure — but the backend can't create the very bucket it stores state in, so `terraform init` fails until the bucket (and, pre-Terraform-1.10, the DynamoDB lock table) already exist. Make them by hand or in a tiny separate bootstrap config with local state, THEN point the backend at them. The failures that stay in: skip the lock and two concurrent `terraform apply`s race and corrupt the state file; and once real state lives in that bucket, a `terraform destroy` of the bootstrap config deletes the bucket out from under everything. Reproducible against LocalStack, no real AWS bill.
rationale: The system-engineer quest report calls out that the quest never explains the S3-bucket + DynamoDB-table remote-backend bootstrap gap; lifehacker has zero Terraform/IaC content of any kind. The 'the backend can't create its own bucket' chicken-and-egg and the missing-lock state corruption are famous, reproducible (LocalStack), on-voice failures — a fresh pillar for the hacks lane.

title: Your CI is red but nothing failed: pytest exits 5 when it collects zero tests
brief: pytest doesn't return 0 for 'ran nothing' — it returns exit code 5, 'no tests collected,' so a fresh `tests/` directory, a typo'd `-k` filter, or a rename that no longer matches `test_*` turns a green suite into a red pipeline with not one failing assertion to point at. Reproduce it in one command against an empty folder and read `echo $?`. The honest fix is to make 'no tests' a deliberate choice: add a real test, fix discovery (file names, `testpaths` in pytest.ini), or, when an empty lane is genuinely fine, allow it explicitly in the wrapper (`pytest ...; [ $? -eq 5 ] && exit 0`) instead of pretending the run passed.
rationale: The quest report's own CI bug is 'pytest tests/unit -q exits code 5 when the directory lacks test files, breaking the pipeline.' lifehacker has CI hacks (step summaries, secrets-in-if, coverage gates) but nothing on pytest's exit codes; the 'red build, zero failures' surprise is famous, one-command reproducible, and on-voice — distinct from the c8 coverage-gate idea.

title: Jekyll ate the {{ }} in your code sample: wrap Liquid examples in raw/endraw
brief: Paste a snippet containing `{{ page.title }}` or `{% if %}` into a Jekyll post and the build runs it as Liquid instead of printing it, so your example renders blank — or the build dies on a tag Liquid can't parse. Wrap the block in a raw/endraw pair so the braces survive to the page. The failures that stay in: forget it and the page can build green while the example is simply gone (verify by rendering, not eyeballing the source), raw doesn't nest so a sample that itself shows an endraw tag closes yours early, and the tags leave stray blank lines unless you trim them. Every case reproducible with a local `bundle exec jekyll build`.
rationale: it-journey's advanced-markdown quest notes in passing that Liquid tags need raw/endraw fencing in Jekyll docs; lifehacker IS a Jekyll site and its markdown hacks cover nested code fences and the markdown tangle but never Liquid executing inside a code block. The 'builds green, example vanished' failure is famous, offline-reproducible, and squarely on-voice — distinct from the nested-fence idea.

title: Fine-tune ResNet on your own images: freeze the backbone, swap the head, and the normalization it silently expects
brief: Transfer learning is the shortcut: load `resnet18(weights=DEFAULT)`, set `requires_grad=False` on the backbone, replace only `net.fc` with a fresh `nn.Linear`, and train the new head on a few hundred images instead of a few million. Two failures stay in — hand the optimizer `net.parameters()` and you either burn compute or (if you forgot to freeze) quietly retrain the whole backbone into mush, so pass it `net.fc.parameters()`; and feed the pretrained net your raw 0–1 images without the exact ImageNet mean/std normalization it was trained on and accuracy craters with no error at all. Reproducible on CPU with torchvision.
rationale: it-journey's computer-vision quest teaches the freeze-and-swap transfer-learning pattern straight; lifehacker's ML ideas are a PyTorch training-loop bug (zero_grad) and token counting, so transfer learning and the silent normalization-mismatch accuracy crater are a distinct, fresh, on-voice failure in the same pillar — no CV hack exists in the backlog.

title: ssh refuses your private key: 'permissions 0644 are too open', chmod 600, and the Windows no-op
brief: Copy an id_ed25519 or a cloud `.pem` key between machines and ssh may slam the door — 'UNPROTECTED PRIVATE KEY FILE ... permissions 0644 are too open' — refusing to use a key any other user on the box could read. `chmod 600 key.pem` (owner read/write only) fixes it, and it's offline-testable: loosen a throwaway key to 644 and watch ssh balk before it ever touches the network. The footgun that stays in: `chmod 400/600` does nothing on native Windows, where NTFS ACLs — not Unix bits — gate the file, so you need `icacls` to strip inherited access or ssh there refuses the key too.
rationale: The security-specialist quest report flags that the quest hands out a `.pem` and says `chmod 400` universally with no explanation and no `icacls` path for Windows. lifehacker has an ssh-config hack (naming servers) and a chmod 644/755 hack, but neither covers ssh's own refusal of a too-open private key or the Windows-ACL gap — a famous, reproducible, on-voice failure that ties both existing threads together.

title: Your CI restored last month's dependencies: the actions/cache restore-keys prefix that serves a stale node_modules
brief: Speed up a workflow by caching `~/.npm` under a key hashed from your lockfile — then meet the footgun that hides in `restore-keys`. On an exact-key miss, restore-keys does a PREFIX match and happily hands you an OLDER cache, so a dependency you just removed lingers because the stale tree still contains it and your build passes on code that shouldn't compile. Too-loose a prefix serves stale, too-tight never hits at all. The fix stays honest: hash the lockfile into the primary key, treat restore-keys as a warm-start only, and run `npm ci` (not `install`) so the lockfile — not the cache — is the source of truth. Reproducible by bumping a dep and watching the prefix restore the old tree.
source_title: Workflow Optimization: Caching and Parallel CI/CD
rationale: it-journey teaches actions/cache keys and restore-keys straight as a speed win; lifehacker's many CI hacks cover permissions, secrets-in-if, step summaries, and coverage gates but never caching or the stale-restore bug. 'Your green build ran on last month's deps' is a real, testable, on-voice failure nothing in the backlog touches.

title: Stop paying for CI runs nobody's waiting on: concurrency + cancel-in-progress (and the one job you must never cancel)
brief: Push three commits in a minute and GitHub runs all three full pipelines — you only care about the last. A top-level `concurrency:` group keyed on the branch ref plus `cancel-in-progress: true` aborts the superseded runs and stops burning minutes. The failure that stays in: aim that same cancel at a deploy or release job and a fresh push can kill it mid-write, leaving a half-published artifact or a tag pointing at nothing — scope the auto-cancel to PR/CI runs and give deploys their own group with `cancel-in-progress: false`. The quieter gotcha: forget the group entirely and cancel-in-progress does nothing at all, because there's nothing for a run to be 'in progress' against.
source_title: Workflow Optimization: Caching and Parallel CI/CD
rationale: it-journey teaches concurrency groups and cancel-in-progress as a cost-discipline win; lifehacker's Actions hacks never cover run cancellation, and the 'cancel-in-progress killed my deploy halfway' footgun is a real, on-voice failure distinct from the caching idea drawn from the same page.

title: Sass can't find your Bootstrap @import: the --load-path=node_modules flag the tutorials leave out
brief: You `npm install bootstrap`, write `@import 'bootstrap'`, run `sass main.scss main.css`, and it dies with `Error: Can't find stylesheet to import` — because Dart Sass does not search `node_modules` by default, and every tutorial that 'just works' had the flag set somewhere off-screen. The fix is one flag: `sass --load-path=node_modules main.scss`. The failures that stay in: the newer `@use 'bootstrap'` needs the exact same load-path (moving off @import doesn't save you), and the Stack Overflow answers telling you to switch to `node-sass` point at a dead, deprecated package — Dart Sass is the live one. Reproducible end to end with `npm i sass bootstrap`.
rationale: The quest report's own high-severity bug is 'Sass example fails with Can't find stylesheet to import without the undocumented --load-path=node_modules flag.' lifehacker has a dark-mode CSS idea queued but nothing on Sass compilation, and the load-path gap plus the dead-node-sass trap are famous, offline-reproducible, on-voice failures.

title: Four numbers instead of a vibe: pull the DORA metrics out of git log and gh (and the one you can't fake)
brief: Stop arguing about whether shipping 'feels' healthy. Three of the four DORA metrics fall out of tools you already have: deployment frequency (`git tag` / `gh release list` counted per week), lead time for changes (the delta from a commit's authored date to the tag that shipped it), and change failure rate + MTTR (from `gh run list` failures and the time to the next green). The honest part that stays in: without an explicit deploy marker in your history the first two are educated guesses, and the metrics measure a SYSTEM, not a person — the moment someone's raise depends on 'deployment frequency,' you get a hundred one-line deploys and a number that went up while nothing got better. Every command runs against a real repo.
rationale: it-journey's kaizen quest teaches DORA metrics and warns against vanity metrics earnestly; lifehacker's meta docs measure its own review-throughput but there's no hack on computing DORA from git+gh. The 'the metric went up, nothing improved' angle is exactly this brand's satire-on-a-comfort-metric, with real, testable commands underneath.

title: No LICENSE file isn't 'free to use' — pick one, and audit the dependency that quietly makes your project GPL
brief: A repo with no LICENSE is all-rights-reserved by default, not public domain, so nobody can legally reuse it — add one (choosealicense.com picks in plain English; `gh repo create --license mit` or a plain `LICENSE` file stamps it). The footgun that stays in: licenses are contagious downward. Pull in one strong-copyleft (GPL/AGPL) dependency and its terms can obligate your entire product to ship source, and it hides deep in the transitive tree where a permissive top-level MIT never warns you. Audit it for real — `pip install pip-licenses && pip-licenses` (or npm `license-checker`) prints every dependency's license so a copyleft one can't ride in unnoticed.
source_title: Open Source Contribution: Maintaining and Licensing
rationale: it-journey teaches permissive-vs-copyleft licensing and the 'no LICENSE ≠ free to reuse' rule straight; lifehacker has deep git/CI/commit-hygiene hacks but nothing on licensing or license auditing. The 'a transitive GPL dep can make YOUR product GPL' gotcha is real, testable with pip-licenses/license-checker, and on-voice — a fresh corner of the same open-source territory.

title: The patch release that broke your build: semver, the caret range that auto-upgrades, and why ^0.x lies
brief: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH is a promise — breaking changes bump MAJOR, features bump MINOR, fixes bump PATCH — and a dependency that ships a breaking change as a 'patch' is the bug you feel three deploys later. The footgun that stays in: the default `^1.2.3` caret range in package.json auto-installs any newer 1.x, so a lockfile-less `npm install` on a fresh machine silently pulls a different minor than your teammate's — and the part everyone gets wrong, `^0.2.3` does NOT allow 0.3.0, because below 1.0 the caret pins to the leftmost non-zero digit (0.x means 'no stability promised'). Commit the lockfile, run `npm ci`, and read the range operator before you trust it. Reproducible with `npm install <pkg>@^0.2.0` and checking what actually landed.
source_title: Open Source Contribution: Maintaining and Licensing
rationale: it-journey teaches semantic versioning and changelogs straight (links semver.org); lifehacker has an HTTP API-versioning hack (410 Gone / Accept headers) but nothing on package semver or npm range operators. The 'breaking change shipped as a patch' and the '^0.x doesn't mean what you think' caret trap are famous, npm-reproducible, on-voice footguns — a distinct topic from the HTTP versioning idea.

title: Stop downloading 5 GB of CUDA to run on a laptop with no GPU: the CPU-only PyTorch wheel index
brief: `pip install torch` pulls the CUDA build by default — around 4.8 GB of GPU runtime you will never touch on a laptop or a CI box that has no GPU. Point pip at the CPU wheel index instead: `pip install torch torchvision --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu` and the download drops to a fraction. The failure that stays in: unpinned tutorial installs also break when a library renames its API out from under you — a fresh `transformers` pulls a version where `pipeline('ner', grouped_entities=True)` is gone, replaced by `aggregation_strategy='simple'` — so pin the versions in requirements.txt AND choose the wheel index on purpose, or 'pip install and follow along' downloads the wrong thing and then runs the wrong thing.
rationale: The quest report's own bugs are an unpinned `pip install torch torchvision` pulling ~4.8 GB of CUDA despite the GPU being optional, and a transformers version bump that broke `grouped_entities`. lifehacker's ML ideas cover the training loop (zero_grad), token counting, and transfer learning but never the environment/install layer. The CPU-wheel index and the version-pin gotcha are real, reproducible, and on-voice — distinct from the existing ML hacks.

title: The cloud VM you deleted is still charging you: kill the orphaned disk, IP, and snapshot the console hides
brief: You spun up a free-tier VM, ran the tutorial, deleted the instance — and the bill kept climbing, because deleting a VM leaves its attached disk, reserved static IP, and snapshots billing on their own. Hunt them for real (`gcloud compute disks list`, `addresses list`, `snapshots list`; the AWS equivalents are orphaned EBS volumes and unattached Elastic IPs) and delete what nothing references. The other footgun that stays in: a billing 'budget alert' does NOT cap spending — it emails you after the money's already gone; there is no server-side stop button, so the only real brakes are deleting resources and scoping the credential that can create them.
source_title: Hello Cloud: First Steps into the Sky Realm
rationale: it-journey warns that 'careless adventurers have been bankrupted by forgotten resources' and teaches billing alerts + resource cleanup straight; lifehacker has zero cloud content. The 'deleting the VM doesn't delete the disk/IP/snapshot' orphan trap and 'an alert isn't a cap' are real, famous, on-voice surprise-bill failures — a fresh pillar for the hacks lane.

title: Your scheduled workflow stopped running: cron is UTC, drifts under load, and GitHub disables it after 60 days of silence
brief: A `schedule:` trigger looks set-and-forget until it isn't. Three surprises stay in: the cron is UTC, not your timezone, so `0 9 * * *` fires at 9am London and lunchtime in New York and you debug a 'wrong time' that was always right; a `* * * * *` every-minute schedule is a lie — GitHub queues scheduled runs on a shared pool and drops or delays them under load, so treat it as best-effort, never a precise clock; and on a repo with no pushes for 60 days GitHub silently disables the scheduled workflow entirely, so the nightly job you were relying on just quietly stopped. The fix stays honest: pick the UTC time on purpose, don't schedule tighter than ~5 minutes, and keep the repo (or the workflow) alive — or move a hard-real-time job off Actions.
rationale: it-journey's action-triggers quest lists `schedule` alongside push/pull_request/workflow_dispatch as a trigger, taught straight; lifehacker has a deep Actions hack shelf (permissions, secrets-in-if, concurrency, caching, self-trigger guards) but nothing on the cron trigger itself. The UTC-not-local, best-effort-timing, and disabled-after-60-days-inactivity surprises are famous, real, and squarely on-voice — the automation that quietly stopped is exactly the brand's 'leave the failure in' payload, and lifehacker IS a scheduled-workflow site.

title: Fork then clone, not clone then confusion: add the upstream remote so your fork doesn't rot
brief: Forking makes a copy you can push to; cloning the original gives you one you can't. Do it in the right order — fork on GitHub, `git clone` YOUR fork (that's `origin`), then `git remote add upstream <original>` — and now `git fetch upstream && git merge upstream/main` (or `gh repo sync`) keeps your copy current. The failures that stay in: a plain `git pull` reads `origin`, not `upstream`, so a fork left alone silently drifts weeks behind and your 'fresh' branch is built on stale code; and opening a PR from a branch you forgot to update means GitHub shows conflicts that are really just your months-old base — the fix is rebasing on an up-to-date `upstream/main` before you push, not editing the diff.
source_title: Hello n00b (GitHub account creation and forking)
rationale: it-journey's hello-noob quest teaches forking earnestly for absolute beginners but stops at 'a fork is a copy'; lifehacker's git shelf is deep (aliases, worktree, reflog, bisect, rebase, merge-conflict) but never covers fork-vs-clone or keeping a fork synced with an upstream remote. The stale-fork drift and the phantom-PR-conflict are famous, fully offline-reproducible (two local repos), on-voice failures — a distinct git topic from everything already queued.

title: Override a theme file in Jekyll without forking the theme: same path wins, and finding the file to copy
brief: A gem-based Jekyll theme (like the one this very site runs) ships its `_layouts`, `_includes`, and `_sass` inside the gem, not your repo — so to change the header you don't fork the theme, you drop a file at the SAME path in your project and Jekyll's lookup prefers yours. The step everyone misses: you can't edit what you can't see, so find the original first with `bundle info --path <theme>` (or `gem contents <theme>`) and copy that exact file in before you change it. The failures that stay in: copy only half an include and the theme's own partials that referenced the other half break; and a theme version bump changes the upstream file you overrode, so your copy silently goes stale and re-introduces the bug the update fixed — pin the theme version and diff on upgrade.
source_title: Frontend: Jekyll Site Building with Bootstrap 5
rationale: it-journey's frontend quest teaches the 'override by placing an identically-named file in your project root rather than forking the theme' rule in one line, straight; lifehacker IS a gem-themed Jekyll site (zer0-mistakes) and its frontend hacks cover navbar/dark-mode/raw-endraw but never theme-file override precedence or how to locate the file to override. The find-it-with-bundle-info step and the stale-override-on-upgrade trap are real, offline-reproducible, and on-voice.

title: One JSON object per line: why JSONL beats a JSON array for logs you append to (and the half-written line a crash leaves)
brief: When you're appending events — agent traces, findings, a build log — a single big JSON array is the wrong shape: every append means parsing the whole file, deleting the closing `]`, and rewriting it, so two writers or one crash mid-write corrupts the lot. JSONL (one complete JSON object per line) lets you append with a plain `>>`, stream it line-by-line without loading it all, and `grep`/`jq -c` each record on its own. The failures that stay in: a process killed mid-append leaves a truncated final line, so every reader must skip a line that won't parse instead of dying on it; and a stray newline inside a value (a pretty-printed object, an embedded `\n`) breaks the one-object-per-line contract, so you write compact and validate each line, not the file as a whole.
rationale: it-journey's observability quest builds its whole audit-log design on JSONL trace files aggregated with jq, used straight; lifehacker runs on JSONL itself (findings.jsonl, this very ideas.jsonl) and has a jq review but no hack on the append-only log FORMAT — why JSONL over a JSON array, and the crash-truncated-last-line and embedded-newline gotchas. Real, offline-testable, and on-voice, and it's the format the site's own harness lives on.

title: curl said 200 and your script marched on: curl exits 0 on a 404 until you pass --fail
brief: A pipeline that does `curl -o out.json https://api/thing` treats a 404 or a 500 as success, because curl only fails on network errors, not HTTP ones — so it happily saves an error page as your data and the build stays green on garbage. Add `-f/--fail` to make curl exit non-zero on a 4xx/5xx, or read the code yourself with `curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}'` and branch on it. The footguns that stay in: plain `--fail` throws away the error body you'd want for debugging (use `--fail-with-body` on modern curl to keep it), and a bare request doesn't follow redirects, so a 301/302 you expected to work returns a 3xx and an empty file until you add `-L`. Testable against any endpoint that returns a chosen status.
source_title: API Fundamentals: HTTP, Requests, and JSON
rationale: it-journey teaches curl (-v/-X/-H/-d/-w) and the 4xx-vs-5xx split straight; lifehacker's HTTP ideas cover API versioning (410 Gone) and retry semantics but never curl's own 'exit 0 on a 404' surprise or --fail/--fail-with-body. It's a famous, script-breaking, easily testable gotcha squarely on-voice and distinct from the retry and versioning hacks.

title: A CHANGELOG humans actually read: the Unreleased section, and why the auto-generated one is your git log in a tie
brief: Keep a hand-curated `CHANGELOG.md` in the Keep a Changelog shape — an `## [Unreleased]` block you add to as you merge, grouped under Added/Changed/Fixed/Removed/Security, each line written for a reader, not a compiler. The honest part that stays in: tools that generate the changelog from conventional-commit messages (semantic-release, release-drafter) emit a wall of 'fix: typo' and 'chore: bump deps' that records WHAT changed and never WHY — fine for machines, noise for humans — so write the release notes on purpose, or at least edit the draft the tool hands you. The other trap: a CHANGELOG and a README that drift apart at release time, so pin the version bump, the git tag, and the changelog entry to one commit.
rationale: it-journey teaches CHANGELOG.md, the Keep a Changelog sections, semver, and release automation (release-drafter/semantic-release) straight; lifehacker's git shelf covers commit hygiene, a conventional-commit hook, and semver ranges but never the changelog itself or the 'auto-generated from commits = noise' honesty. Distinct from the commit-hygiene and semver ideas and on-voice satire of document-everything theater, with the curated Unreleased section as the real payload.

title: 'It works' is not acceptance criteria a robot can grade: writing a Definition of Done a check can evaluate
brief: A Meta take from a site a robot runs: whether a machine can mark a task complete is decided entirely by how you wrote the acceptance criteria. 'It works' and 'looks good' are ungradeable; 'the test suite exits 0', 'file X changed', 'coverage didn't drop', 'the PR is out of draft' are each a signal a github-script check can read as true or false. Turn every criterion into an observable condition, and anything that still needs a human's eye stays exactly that — a labeled human gate, not a fabricated pass. The honest part: the moment a criterion is checkable, an agent can learn to satisfy its letter while missing the point, so the checklist is necessary and never sufficient — some judgement doesn't compress into a boolean.
source_title: The Oracle's Rubric: Agent Success Signals
rationale: it-journey's Oracle's Rubric teaches machine-verifiable acceptance criteria and GitHub completion signals (checks success/failure, pr.draft === false, 'closes #N') straight; lifehacker's meta docs cover how the robot PICKS work, GRADES its own harness, and rates autonomy, but never how a task gets SPECIFIED so a check can grade it. A distinct authoring angle, in conversation with the sister site, and dead-on the self-operating brand.

title: Your no-code two-way sync is stuck in a loop: the update that fires the trigger that fires the update
brief: A Zapier/Make/Power Automate flow that syncs records both directions will happily eat itself: system A updates, which triggers a write to B, which triggers a write back to A, forever — the same self-retrigger loop a bot's own git push causes, just wearing a friendlier UI. The fixes that stay honest: make the sync one-directional unless you truly need both ways, and when you do, add a loop guard (skip the write when the incoming value already matches, or stamp a `last_synced_by` field and ignore your own writes) plus a stable shared key so a re-sync updates a record instead of creating a duplicate. The quieter failure: these platforms fail silently — a broken step just stops and nobody's paged — so wire a failure notification, because 'it hasn't run in three days' is a bug you find in a report, not an alert.
rationale: bash-365's integration guide names the two-way-sync duplicate loop and silent-failure traps straight for a business audience; lifehacker has a GitHub-Action self-trigger-guard hack but nothing on the same loop in low-code iPaaS tools. The 'even no-code has an infinite loop' angle is fresh, reproducible in a free Zapier/Make tier, and on-voice satire of 'no-code means no footguns' — and it's from a brand-new source host the ideas file hasn't drawn on.

title: Put your AI prompts under version control: .prompt.md in git, PR review for prompt changes, and the applyTo glob that silently matches nothing
brief: Stop pasting prompts out of a scratch file. Commit them as `.prompt.md` / `.instructions.md` files so a prompt change is a diff a human reviews in a PR — bisectable, revertable — instead of an untracked edit nobody can trace, and scope each instruction file to the right files with an `applyTo` glob rather than one mega-prompt that fires everywhere. The footgun that stays in: an `applyTo` glob that matches nothing (a leading `/`, `docs/**` when your files live under `_docs/`, a missing `**`) fails silently — the instruction simply never applies and the agent quietly ignores a rule you thought was in force — so verify the glob hits real paths the way you'd test a `.gitignore` pattern. Bonus honesty: small composable prompts are testable in isolation; a 300-line mega-prompt is a black box you can only pray at.
rationale: bash-365's AI-native page teaches prompt versioning, .instructions.md applyTo globs, and composable-over-monolithic prompts under a 'deterministic foundations, AI as an overlay' doctrine — which is lifehacker's own doctrine, making it a direct in-conversation angle. lifehacker's meta docs cover its CI guardrails and the AGENTS.md forbidden-actions gap but never treating prompts as versioned, reviewable, glob-scoped code, and the 'applyTo matches nothing, rule silently off' gotcha is real, testable, and on-voice — from a fresh source host.

title: Decode a JWT in the shell without a library: base64url the middle segment (and why decoding proves nothing)
brief: A JWT is three base64url blobs joined by dots, so you can read the claims with no tooling: `cut -d. -f2 <<<"$JWT" | base64 -d`. The footgun that stays in: the payload is base64URL, not plain base64 — it swaps `+/` for `-_` and drops the `=` padding, so `base64 -d` chokes with 'invalid input' until you translate the chars and re-pad (`tr '_-' '/+'`, then pad the length to a multiple of 4), which is exactly why a naive one-liner fails on a token that decodes fine in a real library. The bigger one: decoding is not verifying — you've read the claims, not checked the signature — so never trust a decoded `exp` or `role` for an auth decision, and never paste a live token into a web decoder, because it's a bearer credential someone else now has.
rationale: The developer quest report peeks inside tokens with `echo "$JWT" | cut -d. -f2 | base64 -d` while teaching JWT auth; lifehacker has no JWT or token-handling content at all. The base64url-not-base64 padding failure and the 'decoded ≠ verified' security point are real, offline-testable, and on-voice — a fresh corner of the hacks lane.

title: redocly lint: the OpenAPI spec checker whose own preview command got deleted out from under the docs
