brief: Honest verdict on Redocly CLI: `redocly lint openapi.yaml` catches the spec errors that quietly become broken clients — missing operationIds, undefined `$ref`s, response schemas that don't match the example — in seconds, and it's the check worth wiring into CI before you publish an API contract. The dealbreakers that stay in: `redocly preview-docs` was removed in current versions, so every tutorial and README that tells you to run it now dies on step one; the default `recommended` ruleset is opinionated enough that a spec someone swore would lint clean still throws a wall of warnings until you tune it; and it's a Node install carrying its own version drift. The free alternative when you don't want the vendor's opinions: `spectral lint` with your own ruleset, or the plain Swagger Editor for eyeballing.
rationale: The developer quest report uses Redocly CLI for OpenAPI linting and its OWN top findings are 'redocly preview-docs no longer exists' and 'a flagship example fails redocly lint despite promising a clean run.' lifehacker's tool lane is all coreutils rewrites with zero API tooling; an OpenAPI linter is fresh territory and the 'the docs tell you to run a command that was deleted' angle is exactly this pillar's honest-verdict promise.

title: Thread one correlation ID through every service (and every CI job) so a failure isn't five unrelated logs
brief: When one request fans out across five services, grepping five separate logs for 'the slow one' is guesswork — mint a correlation ID at the edge (`uuidgen`, or reuse an inbound `X-Request-ID`) and pass it down every hop as a header, so `grep <id> *.log` reassembles the whole trace. The failures that stay in: if each service GENERATES a new ID instead of propagating the one it received, you get five unrelated IDs and no trace at all (propagate, don't regenerate); the header name isn't standardized — `X-Request-ID` vs `X-Correlation-ID` vs the W3C `traceparent` — so one mismatched service silently drops the chain; and in GitHub Actions each job runs in a fresh shell, so an env var set in job A is gone in job B — you hand the ID across via a job `outputs` value or an artifact, not `$CORRELATION_ID`.
source_title: GH-600 in the Wild: Implemented in IT-Journey
rationale: it-journey's GH-600 implementation names 'correlation ID tracing across multi-job executions' as a core observability control; lifehacker's meta docs cover its own harness and JSONL logs but there's no hack on threading a trace ID through services or CI jobs. The propagate-don't-regenerate rule and the 'env vars don't survive across Actions jobs' gotcha are real, testable, and on-voice.

title: Stop arrow-keying across a long command: the readline shortcuts (Ctrl-A/E/W/U, Alt-., Ctrl-x Ctrl-e) and the vi-mode that deletes them
brief: Your shell already ships a text editor's worth of shortcuts — jump to line start/end with Ctrl-A / Ctrl-E, delete the last word with Ctrl-W and the whole line with Ctrl-U, paste the previous command's final argument with Alt-. , and when a line gets truly gnarly, Ctrl-x Ctrl-e opens it in `$EDITOR` to fix and run. All offline, all readline. The failures that stay in: these are the EMACS keymap defaults, so the moment you (or a dotfile) run `set -o vi` they vanish and you're in a different game; Ctrl-S doesn't 'save', it freezes the terminal via flow control (Ctrl-Q thaws it; `stty -ixon` disables the trap so Ctrl-S is free to rebind); and a REPL that doesn't link readline gives you none of them, which is why the same Ctrl-A jumps to line start in bash and prints garbage elsewhere.
rationale: it-journey's cheatsheets index ships a 'Terminal Shortcuts Cheat Sheet' across macOS/Linux/Windows; lifehacker's shell shelf covers aliases, functions, fzf (which rebinds Ctrl-R) and tmux but never the base readline line-editing set. Ctrl-A/E/W/U, Alt-., and Ctrl-x Ctrl-e are famous, offline-testable, and the emacs-vs-vi-mode and Ctrl-S-freezes-the-terminal gotchas are squarely on-voice.

title: Stop giving your app root on the database: a least-privilege MySQL user, and SHOW GRANTS to prove it
brief: The app connects as root because the tutorial did, so one SQL injection owns the whole server. Make a user that can only touch its own schema — `CREATE USER app@'%' IDENTIFIED BY '...'` then `GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON app.* TO app@'%'`, never `ALL PRIVILEGES` — and prove the limit with `SHOW GRANTS FOR app@'%'` before you trust it. Two failures stay in: the one-liner every old tutorial pastes, `GRANT ... ON app.* TO app@'%' IDENTIFIED BY 'pw'`, is a syntax error in MySQL 8 (GRANT no longer creates the user — `CREATE USER` first), and a privilege change never reaches a connection that's already open, so your freshly-locked-down app keeps its old god-mode session until it reconnects. Reproducible in a throwaway Docker MySQL.
rationale: The security-specialist quest report teaches GRANT scoping and SHOW GRANTS verification (SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE vs ALL PRIVILEGES) straight; lifehacker's DB shelf covers query plans, pooling, migrations, JOINs, and schema design but never database user privileges. The 'GRANT doesn't create the user in MySQL 8' and 'privileges don't apply to an open connection' gotchas are real, Docker-testable, and on-voice — a distinct DB topic from everything queued.

title: Verify a download before you run it: sha256sum --check, and why the hash in the docs is a trap
brief: You pulled a release tarball over a network anyone could tamper with — check it against the publisher's hash before you extract and run it: `echo "<hash>  file.tar.gz" | sha256sum --check` prints `file.tar.gz: OK` or a loud `FAILED`. The failures that stay in: the TWO spaces between the hash and the filename are load-bearing (one space and it errors 'improperly formatted checksum line'), a copy-pasted placeholder like `EXPECTED_HASH` always fails because it was never a real hash, and — the honest part — a hash you fetched from the same page as the file only proves the download wasn't corrupted in transit, not that the file wasn't swapped at the source; authenticity needs a signature or a hash from an independent channel. Offline-testable against any file you have.
rationale: The quest report's own gotcha is that `echo "EXPECTED_HASH app-release.tar.gz" | sha256sum --check` fails because the placeholder isn't a real hash. lifehacker has a tar hack and a detect-secrets hack but nothing on verifying a download's checksum. The two-space format trap and the 'a same-page hash proves integrity, not authenticity' point are real, offline-testable, and on-voice — distinct from the tar and secrets ideas.

title: One matrix job failed and killed the other eleven: fail-fast, and the include that adds a job you never listed
brief: `strategy.matrix` fans one job definition into a grid across OS and language versions — but the default `fail-fast: true` cancels every sibling the instant one cell fails, so a flake on node 18 hides whether 20 and 22 were green. Set `fail-fast: false` to let them all finish and read the whole board. The footguns that stay in: `matrix.include` can ADD a combination that isn't in your grid (not only tweak an existing one), so a job you never listed shows up in the run; `exclude` silently drops cells so a 'missing' test was removed on purpose; and each matrix job is its own runner, so a file one cell wrote to disk does not exist for another. Reproducible with a tiny workflow that fails one cell on purpose.
rationale: it-journey teaches matrix builds, needs, and fail-fast straight; lifehacker's deep Actions shelf covers permissions, secrets-in-if, concurrency, caching, step summaries, self-trigger guards, and cron but never the matrix itself. The fail-fast-cancels-siblings surprise and the include-adds-a-job trap are famous, testable, on-voice failures nothing in the backlog touches.

title: Reproduce your whole Mac setup from one file: brew bundle, and the /opt/homebrew PATH gap on Apple Silicon
brief: Stop hand-installing forty tools on a fresh Mac. `brew bundle dump` writes a `Brewfile` of everything you already have, and `brew bundle` on the next machine reinstalls the lot — CLI formulae, GUI casks, even Mac App Store apps — from one committed file. The failure that stays in: on Apple Silicon, Homebrew installs to `/opt/homebrew`, not the Intel `/usr/local`, and the installer does NOT put it on your PATH, so a brand-new terminal answers `brew: command not found` until you add `eval "$(/opt/homebrew/bin/brew shellenv)"` to `~/.zprofile`. The quieter one: most `brew doctor` warnings are advisory, not errors — read them before you start deleting things it mentions.
rationale: it-journey's hello-macOS quest teaches Homebrew install, brew doctor, and bulk-install helper scripts straight; lifehacker's shell/CI shelf has zero Homebrew or machine-provisioning content. The Brewfile-as-reproducible-setup payload plus the famous 'brew isn't on PATH after install on Apple Silicon' gotcha are real, testable, and on-voice — a fresh corner of the hacks lane.

title: Your GitHub Pages site lost all its CSS and every link 404s: the baseurl trap for project sites
brief: The site builds clean, looks perfect on localhost, and deploys as an unstyled wall of text with dead links — because a project site lives at `username.github.io/repo` while `baseurl` in `_config.yml` is still empty. Set `baseurl: "/repo"` (empty is only correct for a user/org `username.github.io` site) and reference every asset through `{{ '/assets/x.css' | relative_url }}` so the prefix is applied everywhere. The failures that stay in: `bundle exec jekyll serve` defaults baseurl to nothing, so the broken build looks flawless locally and only detonates once it's live (serve with the production config to catch it), and a hardcoded `/assets/x.css` that ignores baseurl works on a user site and 404s on a project site. Reproducible with a local `jekyll build`.
source_title: GitHub Pages Portal: Deploying with Jekyll
rationale: it-journey's GitHub Pages quest calls out the empty-vs-'/repo-name' baseurl split as a 404 cause; lifehacker IS a Jekyll site and its frontend shelf covers raw/endraw, theme override, nested fences, and future-dated posts but never the baseurl trap. The 'looks fine on localhost, unstyled and 404ing once live' failure is famous, offline-reproducible, and squarely on-voice — distinct from every Jekyll idea already queued.

title: Stop overloading git checkout: git switch changes branches, git restore un-stages files
brief: `git checkout` does two unrelated jobs — move between branches and throw away file changes — which is why one wrong argument nukes work you meant to keep. The modern split makes intent explicit: `git switch -c feature` creates and moves to a branch, `git switch -` jumps back, and `git restore` handles files (`--staged` un-stages, no flag discards working-tree edits). The failure that stays in: plain `git restore file` is destructive and silent — it overwrites your uncommitted changes with no confirmation and nothing in the reflog to recover, so `--staged` (un-stage, keep edits) and no-flag (discard edits) are one keystroke apart and opposite in blast radius. Every case reproducible in a throwaway repo.
source_title: Git Workflow Mastery: Branches, Merging & Team Collaboration
rationale: it-journey teaches the workflow with `git switch -c` but never explains why switch/restore exist or how restore differs from checkout; lifehacker's deep git shelf (aliases, worktree, reflog, bisect, rebase, merge-conflict) never covers the checkout→switch/restore split. The 'restore discards uncommitted work silently, not in the reflog' footgun is real, offline-reproducible, and on-voice — distinct from the merge-conflict hack drawn from this same page.

title: Your auto-merge workflow waits forever because it's waiting on itself
brief: An auto-merge job that polls `gh pr checks` and merges once everything is green will hang forever the moment it counts ITS OWN run among the checks it's waiting on — a check that can't go green until the job finishes, and the job won't finish until the check is green. The fix is to exclude your own run: grab `$GITHUB_RUN_ID`, filter it out of the check list, and merge when every OTHER check passes. The failures that stay in: match on the run ID, not the job NAME, because two workflows can share a name and you'll silently exclude the wrong one; and guard the empty case — if the only check present is the job's own, 'all checks passed' is vacuously true, so a naive filter would merge a PR nothing ever tested. Add a timeout so a genuinely stuck check fails loud instead of hanging the queue.
source_title: Weaving the Whole: The Serpent Closes the Circle (auto-merge)
rationale: it-journey's ouroboros auto-merge quest names the self-deadlock (a merge workflow waiting on its own status) and the run-ID-not-name fix straight; lifehacker's deep Actions shelf covers permissions, concurrency, caching, cron, matrices, and self-trigger guards but never the auto-merge-waits-on-its-own-check deadlock or the vacuous-empty-checklist merge. Real, testable, and on-voice — the automation that hangs on itself is exactly the brand's 'leave the failure in' payload, and lifehacker runs a gated auto-merge itself.

title: pull_request_target: the trigger that hands your secrets to a stranger's fork
brief: SEVERITY: your whole repo. ATTACK VECTOR: a friendly-looking pull request. The `pull_request` trigger runs fork PRs with a read-only token and no secrets on purpose — so a maintainer 'fixes' the missing secrets by switching to `pull_request_target`, which runs in the BASE repo's context with full secrets and a write token. Do that and then `actions/checkout` the PR's head, and you're executing an attacker's code (a malicious build script, a poisoned dependency) with your credentials in the environment — the classic pwn-request. The three mitigations that actually matter: (1) keep untrusted-code jobs on plain `pull_request`; (2) if you must use `pull_request_target`, never check out or run the PR's code in it — use it only for labeling/triage on trusted files; (3) gate anything privileged behind a manual `environment:` approval and a least-privilege `permissions:` block. Verified by reading which context the token comes from, not by trusting the PR author.
rationale: it-journey's Actions-basics page shows pull_request_target in its trigger syntax without detailing the attack surface (its own text flags the fork-secrets gap); lifehacker's Actions shelf covers permissions scoping, secrets-in-if, and self-trigger guards but never the pull_request_target pwn-request — the single most famous CI RCE. It's Cass Vector's exact beat (a convenience feature that's an attack surface with better marketing), the mitigations are real and sourced, and nothing in the backlog touches it.

title: It works in preview and breaks in production: the JEKYLL_ENV=production gate you forgot you set
brief: Jekyll flips behavior on `JEKYLL_ENV`, which defaults to `development` locally and is set to `production` on GitHub Pages — so anything wrapped in `{% if jekyll.environment == 'production' %}` (analytics, comment widgets, CSS minification, the robots meta) simply does not exist in your local `serve` and only appears once deployed. The failure that stays in: you test the page locally, it's perfect, and the live site loads an analytics snippet or a comments block you never saw render — the one build where you can eyeball it is the one build where that code is switched off. The inverse bites too: a `development`-only debug banner or draft can leak to prod if you gated it on the wrong branch of that `if`. Reproduce both by building twice — `jekyll build` then `JEKYLL_ENV=production jekyll build` — and diffing the output.
source_title: Quest Report: Digital Artist Level 0001 (JEKYLL_ENV production gating)
rationale: The digital-artist quest report flags JEKYLL_ENV=production gating (production-only analytics/minification) as a beginner trap; lifehacker IS a Jekyll site and its frontend/meta shelf covers baseurl, raw/endraw, theme override, and future-dated posts (POST-005) but never the environment gate — the 'looks fine in preview, different in prod' failure is a distinct cousin of the future-flag one, offline-reproducible with two builds, and squarely on-voice.

title: Inject config into a pod without rebuilding the image: ConfigMap as env vars vs a mounted volume (and the one that never updates)
brief: Keep config out of your container image: `kubectl create configmap app-config --from-literal=LOG_LEVEL=info`, then wire it in two ways — `valueFrom.configMapKeyRef` for env vars, or a `configMap` volume mounted as files. The failure that stays in: env vars are frozen at container start, so editing the ConfigMap changes nothing until you `kubectl rollout restart deployment/app`, while a mounted volume syncs the new value into the file on its own (after a short delay) with no restart — pick the injection method by whether you need live reload. The quieter one: a pod that references a ConfigMap or Secret that doesn't exist never starts, it just sits there, so `kubectl describe pod` before you blame your app. Reproducible on kind/minikube.
rationale: lifehacker has zero Kubernetes content — a whole fresh pillar the git/shell/CI/DB hacks never touch (the content-scout skill's own example proposal is even a kubectl one). it-journey teaches ConfigMap/Secret injection straight; the env-var-frozen-at-start vs volume-syncs-live gotcha and the missing-reference pod that never starts are real, reproducible on kind/minikube, and squarely on-voice.

title: Your Kubernetes Secret is base64, not a secret: who can read it, and the three settings that actually protect it
brief: SEVERITY: your whole cluster. ATTACK VECTOR: a value everyone calls a Secret and nobody encrypted. A Kubernetes Secret is base64-ENCODED, not encrypted — `kubectl get secret db-credentials -o jsonpath='{.data.DB_USER}' | base64 -d` hands the value to anyone who can read the object, and by default it sits in etcd in plaintext where a node or backup compromise reads it straight off disk. The three mitigations that actually matter: (1) RBAC — scope `get`/`list` on `secrets` so most accounts and pods can't read them at all (a Role that grants `secrets: [get]` cluster-wide is the real breach); (2) turn on encryption-at-rest for etcd (an `EncryptionConfiguration`, not a checkbox) so a stolen backup isn't a password dump; (3) never `kubectl apply` a Secret manifest from git — the base64 in that YAML is plaintext in your history — create it imperatively or from a sealed/external secrets store. Verified by decoding your own Secret and reading who has RBAC to do the same.
rationale: it-journey's own page warns 'base64 is encoding, not encryption' and points at RBAC + encryption-at-rest; lifehacker has no Kubernetes content, and its one secrets idea (detect-secrets in git history) and MCP PAT-scoping idea never touch cluster Secrets. It's Cass Vector's exact beat — a 'Secret' that isn't secret — the mitigations are real and sourced, and it's a distinct angle from the ConfigMap-injection hack drawn from the same page.

title: Tag the release, forget the changelog, fail the build: a CI gate that ties every version tag to a CHANGELOG entry
brief: Ship versions on purpose: cut an ANNOTATED tag (`git tag -a v1.2.1 -m '...'`, not a bare `git tag v1.2.1`) so the tag carries an author, date, and message — a lightweight tag is just a moving bookmark with none of that — and remember `git push` won't send your tags unless you ask (`git push origin v1.2.1` or `--tags`). Then wire the honest part: a CI step that greps `CHANGELOG.md` for the tag you just pushed and fails the build when there's no matching entry, so an undocumented release can't merge. The failures that stay in: lightweight-vs-annotated bites you later when `git describe` and release tooling ignore the bookmark tags, and a changelog check keyed on an exact string breaks the day someone writes `v1.2.1` in the tag and `1.2.1` in the changelog — normalize before you compare. Reproducible in a throwaway repo.
source_title: Versioning: Semantic Versioning and Release Strategy
rationale: it-journey teaches semver + annotated tags + a CI rule that 'fails if a PR bumps the version tag without a matching changelog entry' straight; lifehacker's existing versioning ideas cover npm caret ranges and writing a good changelog, but never annotated-vs-lightweight tags or the CI gate that enforces tag↔changelog sync. lifehacker IS a CI-gated site, so the enforcement mechanism is a direct in-conversation angle, and both gotchas are real, offline-testable, and on-voice — distinct from the changelog and semver ideas already queued.

title: Build a GitHub-style contribution heatmap from your own git log (and the green squares that quietly lie)
brief: You don't need GitHub to draw the little green calendar: pipe your real history through `git log --date=short --pretty=%ad | sort | uniq -c` to get commits-per-day, then render 52 weeks as a CSS Grid of squares whose `background` steps through five intensity levels set by CSS custom properties — no JavaScript. The failures that stay in: give the grid squares a fixed pixel width and it blows off the screen on a phone until you drop to ~26 columns under a media query; a color-only heatmap is invisible to a screen reader, so each cell needs `role="img"` and an `aria-label` like '3 commits on 2026-01-05'; and the honest punchline — the graph counts commits authored under an email your host recognizes, in ITS timezone, so a real week of work can render as an empty streak because your commits were authored as the wrong user or landed just across a midnight boundary. The squares measure noise; ship anyway, just don't confuse green with productive.
source_title: Contribution Calendar: A CSS Grid Commit Heatmap
rationale: it-journey builds an earnest CSS-Grid contribution heatmap (five intensity levels, aria-labels, a 52→26 column responsive switch) from commit data; lifehacker's frontend shelf has a dark-mode idea and its git-stats idea (the RPG character sheet) turns shortlog into a class/level — this is the distinct visualization angle (the grid itself + accessibility + responsiveness) plus the on-voice 'green squares are a vanity metric that vanish on an email/timezone mismatch' payload. No heatmap or contribution-graph hack exists in the backlog.

title: A prompt without its input is half a receipt: logging the autopilot's runs so a result can be reproduced
brief: A Meta take from a site a robot runs: to audit or reproduce an AI-made change you have to log more than the prompt — you need the exact INPUT snapshot it ran against, the model and version, who ran it, and who approved the result, because the same prompt over a different input produces a different answer and 'here's the prompt' proves nothing. Log at the workflow, not the chat (capture the moment the output enters the repo, not the whole conversation), keep it append-only so an entry can't be quietly rewritten, and keep the person who prompts separate from the person who approves — the same segregation-of-duties an accountant would demand. The honest part, from this exact robot: vendor chat histories have no retention guarantee (assume it's gone when you need it), so the record only exists if YOUR workflow wrote it down at run time — the audit trail you didn't capture is not recoverable later.
source_title: AI Audit Trail: Log Prompts Like Journal Entries
rationale: bash-365 argues AI financial actions need journal-entry-grade audit trails (preparer, date, source-document snapshot, approver) and warns 'prompts without inputs are half a record'; lifehacker IS a self-operating site whose meta docs cover sealing test evidence and versioning prompts (queued) but never the reproducibility gap — logging the input snapshot + model version + approver so an AI change can actually be re-derived. Direct in-conversation angle with the sister consultancy, distinct from the prompt-versioning and JSONL-log ideas already queued.

title: Know which AWS account you're about to nuke: aws sts get-caller-identity, and the region that silently defaults to us-east-1
brief: Before any destructive AWS command, run `aws sts get-caller-identity` to print the account ID, user, and role you're actually operating as — because the same `terraform apply` or `aws s3 rm` hits prod or a sandbox depending on which `AWS_PROFILE`/env vars are live, and the CLI won't warn you which. The footguns that stay in: with no region configured the CLI silently falls back to `us-east-1`, so you create a bucket or an instance in a region you'll never look at again and a later 'not found' is really 'wrong region'; and `aws ec2 describe-availability-zones` is the reminder that a single AZ is one datacenter — 'it's in the cloud' and 'it survives a datacenter losing power' are two different checkmarks.
rationale: it-journey teaches IaaS/PaaS/SaaS, the shared-responsibility model, and shows `aws sts get-caller-identity` / `describe-availability-zones` straight; lifehacker's only cloud hack is orphaned billing resources. The 'which account/region am I actually in' pre-flight, the us-east-1 silent default, and the single-AZ blast radius are real, on-voice footguns nothing in the backlog covers.

title: Your first commit went to a branch GitHub isn't looking at: set init.defaultBranch to main
brief: `git init` still names your first branch `master` on many installs, while GitHub creates repos with `main` — so `git push -u origin main` fails ('src refspec main does not match any') because the branch you committed to is called something else entirely. Set it once with `git config --global init.defaultBranch main`, and rename an existing repo's branch with `git branch -m master main` before you push. The failures that stay in: renaming locally doesn't move the remote — you push the new name, repoint the default on GitHub, then delete the old `master` — and a CI trigger or branch-protection rule pinned to `master` keeps guarding a branch nobody pushes to anymore. Every step reproducible in a throwaway repo.
rationale: The developer quest report's own high-severity bug is the git default-branch mismatch (init produces `master`, docs assume `main`, and `git push -u origin main` fails). lifehacker's deep git shelf (aliases, worktree, reflog, bisect, rebase, switch/restore, merge-conflict) never covers init.defaultBranch or the master→main rename — a famous, offline-reproducible, on-voice first-day footgun.

title: The Jekyll plugin you added to _config.yml and never installed: why your feed and sitemap silently don't exist
brief: Listing `jekyll-feed` (or jekyll-sitemap, jekyll-seo-tag) under `plugins:` in `_config.yml` does nothing on its own — the gem still has to be installed, so `bundle add jekyll-feed` plus a matching Gemfile line is the half everyone forgets, and `bundle exec jekyll build` then quietly produces no `feed.xml` with no error at all. The footguns that stay in: on GitHub Pages only whitelisted plugins run and only via the `github-pages` gem, so a plugin that works locally can vanish on deploy (or the reverse); and the old `gems:` key was renamed to `plugins:` years ago, so a copy-pasted config can file your plugin under a key Jekyll ignores. Verify by checking the built `_site/` actually contains the file, not by trusting a green build.
rationale: The digital-artist quest report's own gotcha is 'jekyll-feed added to config but never bundle-added.' lifehacker IS a Jekyll site and its frontend shelf covers baseurl, raw/endraw, theme override, nested fences, JEKYLL_ENV, and the feed's post limit — but never a plugin declared in _config.yml yet missing from the Gemfile, or the github-pages whitelist. The 'builds green, feed simply isn't there' failure is real, offline-reproducible, and on-voice.

title: Rate-limit your own API: a token bucket in 15 lines, and the limit that quietly multiplies behind a load balancer
brief: Build a token bucket that refills `capacity` tokens at `rate`/second, permits short bursts, and answers an over-limit caller with `429 Too Many Requests` plus honest `RateLimit-Remaining`/`RateLimit-Reset`/`Retry-After` headers so a well-behaved client can slow itself down before you have to reject it. Reproducible in plain Python with a fake clock — no server needed. The footgun that stays in: an in-process limiter set to '100 requests/second' becomes 100×N the moment you run N replicas, because each process counts its own private bucket and nobody counts the total, so the number you advertised is a lie the instant you scale out — the fix is a shared counter (Redis INCR + EXPIRE) so the limit is global. Plus the rate-vs-quota mix-up: a per-second rate never stops one client from burning a whole month's quota in an afternoon.
source_title: Rate Limiting: Token Buckets, 429s, and Quotas
rationale: it-journey teaches token/leaky bucket, 429s, and rate-vs-quota straight. lifehacker's queued API idea (SRC-043, error-handling) is the CLIENT side — honoring Retry-After and backoff — and nothing covers IMPLEMENTING the limiter server-side. The 'your 100/s is really 100×N behind a load balancer' inversion is a real, testable, on-voice failure, and the site's own docs use 'rate limiter' only as a human-review metaphor, never the HTTP one.

title: Your 99% accuracy is a data leak: fit the scaler after the train/test split, not before
brief: That suspiciously great score is usually the model peeking at its own exam. Call `StandardScaler().fit()` on the whole dataset before `train_test_split` and you've leaked the test set's mean and variance into training — the number looks brilliant and means nothing. Fit on the training fold only, or wrap scaler-plus-model in a `Pipeline` so `cross_val_score` re-fits per fold and the leak can't happen. Fully reproducible on CPU with scikit-learn: watch the 'accuracy' fall back to earth the moment you stop cheating. The companion lie that stays in: 95% accuracy on a 95/5 imbalanced set is exactly what you get by always guessing the majority class, so read the `classification_report` precision/recall/F1, not the headline number.
rationale: it-journey teaches train/test discipline, StandardScaler, and cross-validation straight, and names fitting the scaler before the split as data leakage. lifehacker's ML ideas are a PyTorch training-loop bug (zero_grad), token counting, transfer learning, and the CPU wheel index — nothing on the leakage that inflates a score, a universal CPU-reproducible footgun. The 'a comfort metric that's secretly a lie' angle is exactly this brand's payload-under-the-bit.

title: Stop putting your auth token in localStorage: httpOnly cookies, and the CSRF bill they hand you
brief: Any script that runs on your page — including one an XSS hole injected — can read `localStorage.getItem('token')` and walk off with a live bearer credential, because localStorage is readable by all JavaScript on the origin. Store the session token in a cookie set `HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax` instead, so JavaScript can't read it at all and the browser attaches it automatically. Prove the difference in devtools: `document.cookie` shows a normal cookie and stays blind to an HttpOnly one. The trade that stays in: cookies get sent on every request to the origin, so you've closed the XSS-theft door and opened a CSRF one — `SameSite` plus a CSRF token is the other half of the job, not optional — and a token in the URL query string (`?token=...`) is worst of all because it lands in server logs and browser history.
source_title: API Authentication: Keys, Tokens, OAuth2, and JWT
rationale: it-journey teaches token storage straight — httpOnly/Secure/SameSite cookies over localStorage, tokens in headers not URLs — while covering OAuth2/JWT. lifehacker's queued JWT idea is shell-decoding a token (line 71) and there's no hack on WHERE a browser should keep it; the localStorage-is-XSS-readable failure and the 'cookies fix theft but hand you CSRF' trade are real, devtools-demonstrable, and on-voice — distinct from the JWT-decode idea.

title: Get MathJax to render on GitHub Pages: the kramdown that eats your math before the CDN loads
brief: Render real equations on a Jekyll/Pages site by gating a MathJax CDN include on a `mathjax: true` front-matter flag, so only the pages that need it pay the load. The failure that stays in: it renders perfectly on your laptop and breaks the instant GitHub Pages builds it, because kramdown mangles the source before MathJax ever runs — a single-backslash line break in an `align` block collapses unless you quadruple it, an `*` or `_` inside `$...$` gets swallowed as Markdown emphasis and italicizes your formula, and a `$$` block flush against text needs blank lines around it to survive. The fix is escaping or wrapping the math (a fenced `$$...$$` block, or guarded `\(...\)` delimiters) so the Markdown processor leaves it alone. Verify by building, not eyeballing — the one render where it always looks fine is the local one.
rationale: it-journey's cheatsheet wires MathJax into Jekyll via a conditional include and a per-page front-matter flag, straight. lifehacker is itself a Jekyll site with markdown hacks (nested fences, raw/endraw, markdown tangle) but nothing on math rendering, and the 'kramdown ate my backslashes so it works locally and detonates in prod' gotcha mirrors the brand's recurring preview-vs-production failure motif — testable by building, and on-voice.

title: Prove the bug is the theme's, not yours: a minimal reproduction against the bare theme before you file upstream
brief: When your site misbehaves, the honest first question is whether the fault is your code or the framework's — and you answer it by isolation, not by guessing. Build your full site once, then build a single throwaway page against the un-customized theme with its OWN `--source` and `--config` (`bundle exec jekyll build --source repro/ --config repro/_config.yml --destination repro/_site`): if the bug survives with every one of your customizations stripped away, it's upstream and you file it; if it vanishes, the call was coming from inside your repo. The failures that stay in: rebuilding inside your own project doesn't isolate anything (your real `_config.yml`, plugins, and data still load), so the minimal build only proves something when it uses its own source and config; and 'reproduces on my machine' isn't a report until you pin the exact theme commit SHA the maintainer can check out, because a repro against a moving `main` is a repro against nothing.
source_title: The Self-Operating Website 08: The Cartographer (product vs platform bug triage)
rationale: it-journey's Cartographer quest teaches product-vs-platform triage and minimal reproduction straight; lifehacker runs on the same zer0-mistakes theme and its rule is 'theme bugs go upstream, never patched locally' (CLAUDE.md) — but its shelf has only a field note about a build dying on a tag and a threat-model post, no how-to on proving which repo owns a bug. The isolation technique is testable on this very site and the blame-shifting angle ('is it me or the framework? usually you') is on-voice and in-conversation, not a rewrite.

title: Split one messy working tree into atomic commits with git add -p (the staging the 'clean commits' sermon skips)
brief: Everyone preaches 'one logical change per commit,' then a real session leaves a bug fix, a typo, and half a feature tangled across the same files. `git add -p` walks the diff hunk by hunk so you commit them apart: `y`/`n` to stage or skip each hunk, `s` to split one into smaller pieces, `e` to hand-edit exactly which lines go in. You'll know it worked when `git diff --cached` shows only the fix, and `git stash --keep-index` lets you run the tests on precisely what you staged. The failures that stay in: `s` can't split adjacent changed lines with no unchanged line between them — you drop into `e` and edit the patch by hand, and if you miscount the `+`/`-`/context lines the hunk won't apply; and staging half a change can leave a commit that doesn't build, so test the STAGED tree (not your working tree) before you trust that each commit stands on its own.
source_title: Commit Hygiene: Crafting Clean, Atomic Commits
rationale: it-journey's commit-hygiene quest preaches atomic commits as a principle but never shows the tool that produces them from a messy tree, and the git-workflow quest stages whole files with plain `git add` — neither covers `git add -p`. lifehacker already drew rebase -i cleanup and a commit-msg hook from this same page (both about commits AFTER the fact); interactive hunk-staging is the distinct BEFORE-the-commit discipline, fully offline-reproducible, and the 'sermon without the tool' gap is on-voice.

title: yamllint: the linter that fails your file for being 81 columns wide while the real bug is a bare 'yes'
brief: Honest verdict on yamllint: it genuinely catches the YAML that parses wrong before it reaches your build — the `truthy` rule flags bare `on`/`yes`/`no` (the same coercion that turns Norway's `NO` into `false`), and it finds duplicate keys and inconsistent indentation a plain load swallows silently. Worth wiring into CI as `yamllint -c .yamllint .` or the container one-liner `docker run --rm -v "$PWD":/data cytopia/yamllint .`. The dealbreakers that stay in: the default profile is puritanical — `line-length` caps at 80 and `document-start` demands a leading `---` — so out of the box it buries the one real problem under a wall of style nags until you add a `.yamllint` to relax them (or start from `extends: relaxed`); and it lints text, not Jekyll, so it reads a post's `---` front matter as a bare document and warns on files that build perfectly. The free alternative when you only care about validity: a two-line `python3 -c 'import yaml,sys; yaml.safe_load(open(sys.argv[1]))'`, which parses but won't judge your style at all.
rationale: it-journey's YAML quest hands you the yamllint docker one-liner straight as the 'catch errors early' step; lifehacker's tool lane is coreutils rewrites (rg/fd/bat/eza) plus yq — no linter, and yamllint is a different program from yq. The 'fails you for line length while a truthy value is the actual bug' honesty is exactly the tool pillar's promise, and it pairs with the queued Norway-problem hack (the parse gotcha) without duplicating it — this is the tool that catches it.

title: Keep a brag document: the plain-text log of what you shipped that beats your memory at review time
brief: The review-season scramble to remember what you did all year is a losing game against recency bias — you'll list last month's work and forget the fire you put out in March. The fix is a boring append-only file: one line the DAY it happens, git-tracked, each win pinned to a link (the PR, the dashboard, the incident) and phrased as an outcome, not activity. The part that stays in: 'attended 40 meetings' is a diary entry, 'cut deploy time 30% (PR #412)' is evidence — a brag doc full of motion instead of results impresses no one, and the doc written the week before your review is fiction everyone can smell. Certified n00b until it has a number and a link.
source_title: Career Advancement: IC vs Management and Leveling
rationale: it-journey teaches the brag document as a career artifact straight; lifehacker has zero career content — a whole fresh non-CLI corner the git/CI/DB hacks never touch. The bit (performance-review theater, the fake-metrics resume) rides on a genuinely useful, testable habit: append-only markdown in git, one line per outcome with a link. Nothing in the backlog or the queued ideas covers it.

title: Your compose stack says 'up' while the app inside is dead: a healthcheck and depends_on: service_healthy
brief: `depends_on: [db]` only waits for the database CONTAINER to start, not for the database to be READY — so your app boots a half-second early, fails to connect, and crashes on a service that was 'up' the whole time. Add a real `healthcheck:` (run `pg_isready` or curl a `/health` route with `interval`/`retries`/`start_period`) and gate the dependent service with `depends_on: { db: { condition: service_healthy } }` so Compose actually blocks until it's alive. Three footguns stay in: the healthcheck runs INSIDE the container, so the tool it calls (curl, pg_isready) has to be installed in that image or the check fails forever; too short a `start_period` marks a slow-booting service unhealthy and your app never starts; and `condition: service_healthy` needs the Compose-spec map form of `depends_on` — the old list form silently ignores it. Reproducible with two services and `docker compose up`.
rationale: The game-developer 0100 report walks Docker Compose multi-service patterns, volumes, and health checks; lifehacker's Docker ideas cover the daemon error, Dockerfile layer caching, and port-collision scaling but never healthchecks or ordered startup. The 'container is up but the app is dead' startup race is a famous, reproducible, on-voice failure and a distinct topic from every queued Docker hack.

title: continue-on-error kept your CI green while the tests failed: the flag that hides the thing you meant to catch
brief: You drop `continue-on-error: true` on a flaky step so a hiccup doesn't tank the run — and now a genuinely failing step reports success, because Actions records the step's real `outcome` but forces its `conclusion` to success and the job inherits the lie. If you actually care about the result, read `steps.<id>.outcome` in a later step's `if:` and fail on purpose; don't let the whole job swallow it. Two footguns stay in: `continue-on-error` at the JOB level lets an entire broken job report success and any downstream `needs:` treats it as passed; and it's not what you want when you mean 'run this step even after an earlier one failed' — that's `if: always()`, a different tool, so half the uses in the wild are fixing the wrong problem. Reproducible with a two-step workflow where step one exits 1.
rationale: The security-specialist 1011 report teaches GitHub Actions recovery patterns (continue-on-error, needs, checkpoint/retry) as agent-workflow resilience; lifehacker's Actions hacks cover fail-fast, concurrency, secrets-in-if, and step summaries but never continue-on-error masking a real failure or the outcome-vs-conclusion split. The green build that quietly lies is exactly the brand's failure-stays-in payload, reproducible in one small workflow.

title: Attack-tree your own app: draw the goal, branch the ways in, kill the cheapest leaf first
brief: Put the attacker's GOAL at the root ('read another user's data'), branch every path to it with AND/OR logic down to concrete leaves ('steal a session cookie', 'increment the sequential ID in the URL', 'SQL-inject the search box'), then defend the CHEAPEST viable leaf first — the one anyone can run from the address bar, not the Hollywood one. Yes, a nation-state could bribe your hosting provider; the integer `/invoice/1042` a stranger can retype to `1043` is a $0 attack and it's the one that ships breaches. Three mitigations stay in: fix the cheapest leaf, never the scariest; label the AND-branches (both conditions required), because that's the one spot where a single control breaks the whole path; and a tree you drew once is a diagram, not a defense — recut it the day the app grows a new door.
rationale: it-journey's threat-modeling quest teaches STRIDE, DFDs, AND attack trees; lifehacker has a queued STRIDE hack (a different technique — categorize what could go wrong) but nothing on attack trees, which decompose one goal into the cheapest path in. Cass's 'escalate to the absurd worst case, then hand you the leaf that actually matters' voice maps exactly onto the cheapest-viable-leaf method — on-voice, testable against any real app, and distinct from the STRIDE idea already queued from this same source.
